articles.title_orig: Nixon had a tell when he lied. His lawyer told Bob Woodward all about it.
articles.title_zh: Nixon had a tell when he lied. His lawyer told Bob Woodward all about it.
articles.content_orig:
Author and investigative journalist Bob Woodward at his home in Washington on Friday, Nov. 20, 2026. J. Scott Applewhite/AP hide caption
For more than half a century, Bob Woodward entered people's lives as they rose to power and left behind his draft of history.
"I think I've never ended an interview," Woodward told Morning Edition . There were always more questions to ask.
Now, at 83, he's answering some questions about himself — the experiences that shaped him, the decisions he made as a journalist and what he might have gotten wrong.
Woodward is the reporter who, with Carl Bernstein, exposed the Watergate scandal that brought down President Richard Nixon. He has written revelatory books about presidents ever since.
In his new book, Secrets: A Reporter's Memoir , released Tuesday, Woodward turns his attention to the secrets of his own life. A broken family. Chance encounters that changed his career. Sources who trusted him. Stories he didn't get right.
After 55 years at The Washington Post , he also reflects on what it takes to do good journalism — and what stands in its way today.
The reporter also chooses to reveal some of the anonymous sources who gave him information — a decision that raises ethical questions about protecting confidential sources after their deaths.
"I thought this was a time to let people know. And these are people who didn't do bad things. Actually, they were people who were trying to get the true story out," Woodward said.
In some cases, the sources are dead now. In others, they gave permission.
It's common in Washington to think that people who feed reporters information get better coverage, though some of Woodward's books complicate that idea.
His book about Bill Clinton's administration described a chaotic and dysfunctional White House. Looking back decades later, Woodward says he missed a larger story: the peace and prosperity of Clinton's presidency.
"I didn't see that at the time, and that's my fault," he said.
In the run-up to the Iraq War, Woodward buried in the 16th paragraph of a story an admission from Bush administration officials that they had no smoking gun on Iraq's alleged weapons of mass destruction.
"That should have been the lead," he said.
Journalists Carl Bernstein, second from left, and Bob Woodward, second from right, are flanked by actors Dustin Hoffman, left, and Robert Redford, right, at the premiere of All the President's Men in Washington on April 5, 1976. AP hide caption
In the memoir, Woodward recalls how he and Bernstein could spend two or three weeks on a single story during Watergate. He worries that the internet has fostered a culture of impatience at the expense of in-depth reporting.
"The secret to impactful reporting is time," he writes.
Woodward also criticizes Washington Post owner Jeff Bezos for remaining silent on President Trump's attacks on the press, while noting that, to his knowledge, Bezos has not interfered in the newspaper's news operation.
"An owner is supposed to be a custodian of uncompromising reporting," Woodward writes.
Woodward traces his investigative reporting back more than 70 years to when he was a child in Wheaton, Ill.
"My family was fracturing right before me. My mother ran off with my father's best friend," Woodward told Morning Edition .
He found out about his parents' divorce by looking in his father's sock drawer.
"Find the sock drawer and look there," he said.
Woodward became a reporter after serving in the Navy. He says he was accepted to Harvard Law School and turned that down to work for a weekly newspaper. His father, a lawyer and a judge, told him: "You're crazy."
What is so great about being a reporter that he wanted to do it?
"That you get to make momentary entries into people's lives when they're interesting, and then get the hell out when they cease to be interesting, which is what always happens," Woodward said.
Woodward came by NPR's studios accompanied by an aide who held a cane in case he needed it.
As technology transforms journalism and the pressures on reporters mount, Woodward's approach to reporting remains rooted in human connection.
"I will continue to show up and knock on doors, even with a cane in my hand," he writes in the book's closing pages.
Later today, you can watch our extended video conversation with Bob Woodward exclusively in the NPR app. You'll find it in the "Video" tab. And if you don't have the app, download it now at npr.org/gettheapp .
The radio interview was edited by Adriana Gallardo. The digital version was produced by Majd Al-Waheidi and edited by Suzanne Nuyen.
A previous web description for the audio version of this story incorrectly referred to Bob Woodward's memoir as Secrets: A Reporting Memoir. The title is Secrets: A Reporter's Memoir .

articles.title_orig: Trump’s push to restore Nvidia CEO could haunt the company in Congress
articles.title_zh: Trump’s push to restore Nvidia CEO could haunt the company in Congress
articles.content_orig:
One of the most dramatic about-faces in corporate America's history, Jensen Huang's return to the helm of AI chipmaker Nvidia spurred an equally historic record in the options market. More than 11 million options contracts traded on Nvidia stock Monday, the most active single day of trading for the stock's options in history. That outpaces the 9 million options traded on the Invesco QQQ Trust , and compares to 14 million traded on the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (SPY) . Despite Nvidia's monstrous 31% rally and options volume that was more than five times the 30-day average, positioning in the flows was not abnormally bullish. Of the top 10 trades by dollar amount, two big put sales stood out, but there were no likely outright call buys, based on data from Barchart and SpotGamma. If there was speculative call-buying, it was dwarfed by big trades between the 160 and 170 strikes, where four million options traded for almost $2 billion.
Nvidia closed near $165. "People are mostly just trying to collect a lot of premiums through short vol trades and rolls once they heard about Jensen Huang, take advantage of the vol drop more than anything else," Jason DeLorenzo, founder of Volland, an options-analytics software, said by phone. "It seems like options traders were all repricing, which created record volume, but did not create any obvious one-sidedness." Just under 6.7 million calls traded versus 4.3 million puts, according to Cboe LiveVol data. About 2.4 million calls were likely initiated by buyers, compared with 1.6 million purchasing puts, exchange data show. Open interest in calls was highest at the 170-strike, while open interest in puts was highest at the 150-strike, Barchart data show.

articles.title_orig: Too Big to Fire? Jensen Huang Is Back at Nvidia; Questions Loom Over AI Boom & U.S.-China Relations - Democracy Now!
articles.title_zh: Too Big to Fire? Jensen Huang Is Back at Nvidia; Questions Loom Over AI Boom & U.S.-China Relations - Democracy Now!
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang 's return as Nvidia CEO may have eased concerns over the chipmaker's leadership, but it has also brought renewed scrutiny to the company's corporate governance and its reliance on its founder.
Huang's abrupt departure and unexpected reinstatement exposed a deeper vulnerability at the heart of Nvidia, industry experts told CNBC, raising questions about board oversight and succession planning.
"What does it mean if you have a company too big to fail or a CEO too big to fire?" Angela Mancini, head of advisory for global risk insights at Dow Jones, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia " on Tuesday.
Mancini pointed to Huang's unusually large number of direct reports as another sign of how heavily Nvidia depends on its founder.
"What does it mean when someone has 60 direct reports, and you literally are in a situation where you feel like you can't fire them?" she added.
Nvidia's market cap ballooned from $3 trillion on Friday to almost $4 trillion on Tuesday after Huang was reinstated. "That is what you'd call a founder premium," Yang Wang, a principal analyst at Counterpoint Research, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe."
"The reaction has been staggering," Wang said. "But is this level of dependence healthy?"
For Nvidia, Huang's return offers an opportunity to address some of the governance issues brought to light by his departure.
Jeff Herbst, managing partner at GFT Ventures and a former Nvidia executive who spent nearly two decades at the company, said he had written to the board late last week calling for Huang's return.
While initially disappointed by the allegations surrounding Huang, Herbst said he came to view the episode as an opportunity for Nvidia to strengthen its governance, succession planning and overall management.
"While a lot of people saw a crisis here, I saw a potential opportunity," he said.
Herbst said Nvidia's management and oversight functions needed to evolve alongside its transformation from a relatively small technology company into one of the world's largest corporations.
"I think the corporate governance, the succession planning, the legal function, the regulatory function, the political function, all has to scale at the same time," he said.
He suggested Nvidia add more experience to its board by bringing in individuals who have run large companies and take a more formal approach to developing potential successors to Huang.
Tom Hulick, CEO of Strategy Asset Managers, agreed, saying the chip giant's "corporate governance definitely needs to be retooled."
It's "unheard of" and "unprecedented" for a president to enforce the reinstatement of a company's CEO, Hulick said on "Squawk Box Europe" on Tuesday.
"He's a born leader. He's enduring a lot of pain right now. Does he deserve to be back as CEO? It's not for me to speculate. Is he the right person? Probably for now."
However, Hulick added that the company still has "a lot of things to worry about" regarding corporate governance.
Huang's departure also exposed how closely Nvidia's leadership and long-term strategy are tied to its founder, raising questions about how the company would navigate a future transition.
Stacy Rasgon, managing director and senior U.S. semiconductor analyst at Bernstein Research, said the episode had revived attention to a risk investors had long overlooked.
"We all knew that there was key man risk here. We all chose, and I'm including myself in that. We all kind of chose to just ignore it," Rasgon told CNBC.
Succession planning, he said, is an issue both Huang and the board will need to address and communicate clearly to investors.
"I think both Jensen and the board will have to figure out, and I think communicate to investors," he added.
Herbst also pointed to Huang's personal role in driving Nvidia's technological innovations, including his willingness to invest in artificial intelligence and high-performance computing long before those businesses became profitable.
New markets such as autonomous systems and robotics would require major investment and a leader with Huang's passion and vision, Herbst added.
Correction: This story has been updated to reflect that Angela Mancini said Nvidia is in a situation where it feels like you can not fire the CEO.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia stock falls after epic rally on Jensen Huang's return as CEO
articles.title_zh: Nvidia stock falls after epic rally on Jensen Huang's return as CEO
articles.content_orig:
How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO
Shares in Nvidia dipped on Tuesday as US politicans questioned President Donald Trump's role in the return of Jensen Huang as chief executive.
Huang was handed back his job at the AI microchip maker on Monday less than two weeks after he was forced to resign following the revelations of extra marital affairs, one of which was with a suspected Chinese spy.
Trump has said he played a big role in the 63-year-old's reinstatment, which has led to questions and backlash from US lawmakers.
While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the annoucement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.
The company's share price was down almost 8% on Tuesday, but remained well above the level it closed at on Friday, before Huang's shock return was revealed.
However, Nvidia was not the only semiconductor chip company to experience share price declines on Tuesday, with rival AMD down more than 10%.
Broadcom and Marvell Technology shares were also lower, suggesting that investors were continuing to weigh up concerns over potential regulation by newly-elected Democrats, as well as the central question as to whether the huge amounts being invested in AI will pay off.
Nvidia's share price for example, is down almost 30% over the past six months and had been on the decline before the scandal involving its co-founder emerged earlier this month.
The company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn on its original position. Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.
Trump said he had spoken to the company's directors and convinced them to bring back Huang.
"They did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump told CNBC. "And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot."
There has been bipartisan political anger over Huang's reinstatement.
Republican representative Don Bacon said Nvidia should have "ignored the Administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang", while Republican senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips".
Democratic representative Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump's "direct involvement" with Nvidia's decision "raises serious national security and corruption questions", and Democratic senator Ruben Gallego said Congress needed to "investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement".
Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where the Nvidia boss will be questioned over his relationship with Alice Huang, alleged to be a spy for China, due to national security concerns.
The US Commerce Department announced it was preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer where Alice Huang (no relation) was chief executive. China has denied the spying allegations.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic shares tumble below $83 IPO price, on track to lose nearly $200 billion in value
articles.title_zh: Anthropic shares tumble below $83 IPO price, on track to lose nearly $200 billion in value
articles.content_orig:
Shares of Anthropic fell 8% on Tuesday, sending the stock below the artificial intelligence company's $83 IPO price.
The AI lab's stock has been sinking steadily since opening at $111.50 on the Nasdaq on Thursday, after Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in the largest offering of all time. Investors eagerly awaited Anthropic's debut in hopes that the company would revitalize the broader AI trade, which has been volatile in recent weeks over concerns about the feasibility of a multitrillion-dollar infrastructure buildout.
Anthropic's initial public offering was oversubscribed, and roughly half of the institutional investors that placed orders for the stock were left empty-handed, as CNBC previously reported . But at least for now, as the market wavers, those firms don't appear to be racing to scoop up shares.
Chip stocks Nvidia , Advanced Micro Devices and Intel , as well as neoclouds CoreWeave , IREN and Nebius , all fell during intraday trading on Tuesday. The market is still reeling after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, a dramatic reversal from his ouster earlier this month. Nvidia shares surged more than 30% on Monday, but pared those gains Tuesday.
Analysts at Canaccord Genuity said Tuesday that they're focused on Anthropic's long-term potential. They said they believe that the company is building "one of the most important enterprise technology franchises of the AI era" and that the "opportunity is considerably larger than traditional software spending."
Canaccord Genuity initiated coverage of Anthropic with a buy rating and a $135 price target.
"The risks are unusually large, particularly around infrastructure commitments and the durability of competitive differentiation, but we believe the combination of exceptional growth, emerging earnings capacity, and an attractive entry valuation support a compelling investment opportunity," the analysts wrote in a Tuesday note.
Wedbush analysts initiated coverage of Anthropic with an outperform rating and a $120 price target on Monday. They said Anthropic went public in a "tumultuous market" as debate around the AI buildout continues, but that they expect the company to navigate the competitive environment and "capture a uniquely large addressable market."
"While there's going to continue to be many ups and downs, and winners and losers as this ecosystem gets built, in our view there is no real question that it does get built over time," the analysts wrote in a Monday note. "The genie is out of the bottle. And ANT is a strong play on that theme."
Analysts at Oppenheimer initiated coverage of Anthropic with an outperform rating on Tuesday, and they set a $150 price target for the stock.
They said their "bullish stance" on the company stems from their belief that Anthropic will capture growing enterprise AI spending, that its improving compute efficiency lowers cost per task and that its multi-chip strategy optimizes price performance. The analysts added that Anthropic's focus on the enterprise also relies less on consumer subsidies, and that rising customer adoption creates "a substantial runway" for the company.
"While competition and compute commitments remain risks, we believe Anthropic can translate its leadership into durable growth and operating leverage," the analysts wrote in a Tuesday note.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Microsoft declares 'Code Red' after historic outage, internal memos show
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Microsoft declares 'Code Red' after historic outage, internal memos show
articles.content_orig:
July bug overwhelmed newer servers, prompting promises of stronger safeguards and faster recovery
Some emails never reached their recipients during November's Microsoft 365 outage, the company has confirmed in a final report that also exposes gaps in its testing and recovery procedures.
The post-incident report details how a Windows defect brought down Exchange Online and disrupted features across other Microsoft 365 services. For affected users, the cloud became someone else's unavailable computer.
A preliminary report had already blamed a July code change, combined with a failover and reduced capacity. The final report confirms those findings and sets out Microsoft's plans to improve change auditing and recovery procedures, and add spare capacity. The defect affected Microsoft's gateway server configuration, not standard Windows deployments.
The epic outage (named the "Microsoft long weekend" by some wags) kicked off on November 12 and wasn't fully resolved until November 14.
Microsoft extended its delivery retry window to 48 hours, but some delayed messages destined for consumer mailboxes inactive for more than 30 days still expired, generating non-delivery reports. The company said all queued enterprise messages were eventually delivered, with none found permanently lost.
The report is grim, particularly in how the failure ramped up as US users came online to find gateway servers toppling over. At the worst point, more than 80 percent of North American gateway servers were unresponsive.
The problem proved elusive, and it took Microsoft some time to identify the change and deploy a fix.
Microsoft has had a week to ponder what it did and did not do, and the report has some next steps to avoid a repeat of November's events. Some are obvious, and some are a little surprising.
Working to reduce the blast radius of failures is an obvious one, and actions include partitioning and isolation to ensure failures can be contained before taking down traffic globally. Recovery procedures also need improvement, along with communication and capacity to ensure there is sufficient headroom.
Microsoft's load tests used older, lower-core-count hardware, making them less likely to expose a defect that worsened on newer machines. The company now plans to test newer hardware with more realistic traffic and peak loads, and broaden its failover testing.
Microsoft also plans to improve diagnostics and change auditing so engineers can identify troublesome Windows changes faster. July's defect had been running worldwide for more than three months before it brought the gateways down. ®

articles.title_orig: Nvidia CEO Faces Senate Scrutiny Over China Chip and Spy Scandal
articles.title_zh: Nvidia CEO Faces Senate Scrutiny Over China Chip and Spy Scandal
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of AI tech giant Nvidia effective immediately following a scandal involving an alleged spy, the company's board of directors announced Thursday.
The decision came amid an investigation into Huang's affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspect was spying for China. President Trump said this week the FBI is investigating romantic and business ties between Huang and suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang. The two aren't related.
Nvidia's board had been preparing to oust Huang , two sources familiar with the matter confirmed to CBS News on Wednesday night, plans that were first reported by the Wall Street Journal.
Huang's departure also follows a New York Times report Wednesday that five employees at Nvidia came forward alleging Huang was romantically involved with a subordinate, Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare.
The Times also reported Huang and Powell, who are both married to other people, were caught on video being affectionate at a conference in March, according to two Nvidia employees. The Times has not seen the video and CBS News has not verified the report.
After Huang's resignation was announced Thursday, the Reuters news agency reported that Huang also had an intimate relationship with a second employee, according to two people familiar with the matter. The agency only identified the employee as a woman.
The company's interim CEO will be Colette Kress, who is currently Nvidia's chief financial officer and will continue in that role.
"The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," Harvey Jones, who was announced as the company's first board chair, said in a statement.
Kress has been Nvidia's CFO since she joined the company in 2013. She previously worked in finance roles at tech companies like Cisco and Microsoft for nearly 25 years.
Nvidia was co-founded by Huang in 1993. It became one of the most valuable companies in the world by designing the powerful semiconductors that fuel many of the world's leading AI firms, making its technology highly sensitive and subject to export controls limiting sales to China.
Nvidia's stock plunged as news emerged of the company's turmoil, potentially erasing almost $500 billion in value. In Thursday's trading, the stock price closed down 4.3% at $166.19.
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was an executive at Megaspeed International , a Singapore-based data center company whose website touts its partnership with Nvidia.
Megaspeed grew with the help of access to Nvidia's restricted AI computer chips. According to U.S. investigators, Alice Huang was able to gain access to 240,000 chips that were banned from being exported to China. Megaspeed is under investigation in the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China.
In Washington, top Democrats on Capitol Hill have expressed concerns over whether Jensen Huang's ties to Alice Huang may have compromised U.S. national security.
Following Jensen Huang's resignation, Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts said his departure doesn't absolve him or the company from the scandal.
"Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and NVIDIA's board of directors still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Warren said in a statement.
Before Huang resigned, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., told CBS News the departure could help China in the competition between Beijing and the U.S.
"With him out as CEO, China could significantly narrow the gap versus the U.S.," Ives said. He added: "The problem now is that there's no replacement for Jensen. It's a black eye moment for him, for Nvidia, and actually the U.S. tech industry. I'd say it's dark day for, you know, U.S. technology."
Following Thursday morning's announcement, Mr. Trump said on his Truth Social platform that there was "only one man" who could replace Huang: former Apple CEO Tim Cook .
Mr. Trump had a close relationship with Huang, who has attended AI-focused White House events and traveled with Mr. Trump to China. Late last year, Mr. Trump granted Nvidia the right to sell advanced H200 chips to "approved customers" in China, with the U.S. government getting a 25% cut — a major coup for Huang, who has long sought to sell more technology to the Chinese market. The deal did not cover Nvidia's even more advanced Blackwell and Rubin systems.
In a radio interview Thursday, Mr. Trump brought up that he gave Huang a National Medal of Science earlier this year. "What a horrible thing that is," he said of the situation involving Huang, adding, "That's so sad to see that happen."
In a statement accompanying her appointment as interim CEO, Kress said that the company's focus will be on "serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders."
"NVIDIA's strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years," Kress said.
The board said it will be conducting a search for a permanent CEO and will consider internal and external candidates.
Isabel  Vincent , Jennifer  Jacobs , Aimee  Picchi and Jo Ling  Kent contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: ‘Menacing eyes’: Pope Francis’s diary details three encounters with the devil
articles.title_zh: ‘Menacing eyes’: Pope Francis’s diary details three encounters with the devil
articles.content_orig:
Pope Francis suffered a spiritual crisis during his papacy in which he saw visions of the devil and hell while struggling with how to exercise power, newly published diaries of the late pontiff reveal.
The Argentine pope intermittently kept a diary between 1992 and 2024, first during his time as a bishop in Argentina and then following his election as pope. Now, several of those entries have been compiled in a book published on Tuesday. It was written by Cardinal Víctor Manuel Fernández, one of Francis’ closest aides and a fellow Argentine, who offers a detailed commentary on the papal diaries.
The 160-page “The Private Diary of Pope Francis” is focused primarily on the pope’s spiritual life and pastoral agenda, although it also details how the first Latin American pope struggled with temptations connected to the use of power in 2021-2022. It also includes what the pope describes as encounters with the devil along with his thoughts about his successor, Leo XIV, whom he characterized as “irreproachable.”
The publication of papal diaries is rare, but not unprecedented, and can provide unusually personal insights. While some popes order that their personal papers be destroyed, the diaries of John XXIII were published posthumously, as were some papers of John Paul II.
Francis wrote 86 pages of the black-covered diary — initially a planner for the year 1992 — while he was in Argentina and 55 pages while he was pope. “He showed me a few books, including what looked like an old agenda book with a leather cover. When he opened it, I saw that it was filled with notes in his handwriting. He told me, ‘From this, you will all see,’” Fernández wrote.
Here are some of the major revelations:
The diaries say that the pope experienced “frequent demonic attacks,” and Francis details three encounters with the devil: two while he was archbishop of Buenos Aires and another in 2018, when he was pope. Francis wrote that the devil has “eyes of fire,” also describing them as “menacing” and “seductive” eyes.
“I can’t forget his eyes the first two times — from the car when I was returning to the house, and in the choir loft during Mass. However, he always reappears in different situations,” the pope wrote in an entry for August 18, 2024. The third occasion came after returning from a visit to Chile in 2018, a trip overshadowed by the clerical sexual abuse scandal.
“On one occasion, a few days after returning to Rome, I was in a meeting. I saw him and heard his voice [his underlining], triumphant, possessing everything: ‘Now I’ve gotten everything I wanted,’” the pope wrote on January 24, 2021. “Just as I can’t forget his eyes from the previous two, in this case, I can’t forget the powerful raspiness of his voice. The Lord granted me an opportunity to leave that meeting, and he thus freed me.”
Catholic teaching holds that the devil is a fallen angel and a real presence, and Catholic tradition cautions that those who are serious about attaining holiness will often encounter strong spiritual opposition. During his pontificate, Francis would frequently mention the devil, linking it to gossip and money. “The devil enters through the pockets,” he often said.
The diary also includes details of how Francis believed God spoke to him in dreams. On one occasion, Francis recounted seeing “the entrance to hell.” The pope, in 2018, described it as a form of “pagan seduction in full force,” an apparent reference to the worshipping of idols. “I peeked in to look a little and it terrified me. It was before going to sleep. I grabbed the rosary as a weapon. I thank the Lord for this help,” he wrote.
The book reveals that in 2021-2022, Francis underwent a spiritual crisis connected to a temptation or “curiosity” with power and which was partly connected to excessive activity and feelings of self-sufficiency. It was, the pope explained, also linked to “governance issues, pressure regarding decisions to make, and aridity and desolation.”
To counter the temptation, he sought to exercise greater humility and patience, even leaving people in place in the church’s central administration who others felt were undermining his papacy. During his 12-year pontificate, Francis, initiated several reforms in the church, including on the treatment of LGBTQ Catholics and the role of women, but faced significant opposition. Some of it came from inside the Vatican, where some bishops and cardinals openly resisted his reforms.
The Pope Francis I knew: Reflections from CNN’s Vatican correspondent
“One time in my presence, a bishop asked him why he had not yet fired someone in the Roman Curia who had been speaking badly of him in public and pursuing a personal agenda very different than his,” wrote Cardinal Fernández, who was appointed by Francis to lead the Vatican’s doctrine office. “After an interminable silence, he responded by explaining that he felt a strong sensation in his heart that God did not want him to become a puppeteer who uses and manipulates people according to his own convenience. He explained that, for this reason, he preferred to let that person remain in his position.”
While the diary doesn’t go into specific examples, the pope wrote on December 30, 2022, that he refused the temptation to treat “others like puppets.” In 2018, he said that “this sense of self-sufficiency and I can solve everything brought me to the gates of hell. I can’t forget the day I saw it.”
The crisis that Francis underwent, Fernández explained, was “connected to power” and the curiosity to “discover what it is like to exercise one’s own power.” As a member of the Jesuit religious order, the pope was continuously engaged in a spiritual discernment, essentially engaging in self-examination to determine whether he was working for self-interest or the good of others.
For Francis, feeling that he was “above the world” through his power was “the path of the worst spiritual worldliness imaginable, which he sought to dismantle by avoiding every symbol or expression of papal ‘majesty’ or ‘glory,’” Fernández added.
During his pontificate, Francis adopted a simple style, living in a Vatican guesthouse, wearing black orthopedic shoes and refusing certain papal vestments.
While the diaries focus on the pope’s spiritual life, they do include comments about the clerical sexual abuse crisis, including in Chile in 2018. At the time, Francis was criticized for dismissing the case of a bishop who had been accused of witnessing and covering up abuse when he was a priest. The pope later apologized for his handling of the case and summoned all the bishops from the country to Rome. In an unprecedented move, the bishops offered their resignations to the pope en masse .
“Devastated because of the situation in Chile and the dialogue with the journalists on the airplane. I fell off the cot then,” Francis wrote. “It was hard for me to admit what happened in Chile; I didn’t think it was so serious.” The phrase “fell off the cot,” the book explains, means to suddenly wake up to something. Francis would go on to make several reforms aimed at tackling clerical sexual abuse.
The diaries reveal the pope’s thoughts on Cardinal Robert Prevost, the future Pope Leo XIV, whom Francis brought to the Vatican to lead the department for appointing bishops. According to Fernández, Francis called Prevost “a great pastor, a generous missionary, and an irreproachable man.”
He was also generous to his critics, including Cardinals Robert Sarah, a Guinean, and Gerhard Muller, a German prelate. The Argentine pontiff said Sarah had “a refined spiritual sensitivity” and that Muller “seems aggressive but he’s a good man,” Fernández wrote.
The diaries reveal Pope Francis’ dedication to his ministry, frequently mentioning feelings of exhaustion, both in Argentina and after his election. Francis rarely took a day off and never went on vacation outside the Vatican. In 2019, he described himself as “feeling exhausted, almost without spiritual support and without a point of referen

articles.title_orig: CF40 Research: China’s real estate adjustment may be nearing its end—and its external surplus could stop widening
articles.title_zh: CF40 Research: China’s real estate adjustment may be nearing its end—and its external surplus could stop widening
articles.content_orig:
Late last month, CF40 Research , the research arm of the China Finance 40 Forum-a leading non-governmental think tank specializing in economics, shared its annual flagship report, China’s Economy: Toward a New Paradigm—Drivers, Trends, and Policy Implications , at its 2026 Bund Summit .
Guo Kai , President of CF40 Research and a former Chinese central bank official, kindly shared a copy and allowed me to share an excerpt.
The following passages are from the report’s English text. They have been rearranged and intervening material omitted; section headings and this introduction are mine. Corporate debt and profit figures below refer to its sample of A-share-listed companies outside finance and petroleum.
By 2026, the current real estate adjustment may not yet have fully run its course, but signs of structural stabilization have begun to emerge. After five years of deep adjustment, housing sales, investment, inventories, and developers’ balance sheets have entered a new phase, while house-price declines have begun to moderate. Few would expect the real estate sector to return to its former “golden age,” but the drag from the ongoing adjustment on the economy has diminished markedly at the margin. In other words, real estate is gradually shifting from the economy’s largest source of downward pressure toward a more stable influence.
Based on our analysis of international real estate corrections, China’s current real estate adjustment has already been considerable in both duration and magnitude, and the market has likely entered a bottoming phase. Further adjustment remains possible, but another sharp contraction appears unlikely.
Since the start of 2026, China’s real estate market has begun to show signs of “structural stabilization.” We selected 33 core cities for analysis, including the four first-tier cities—Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, and Shenzhen—and major second-tier cities such as Hangzhou, Suzhou, Qingdao, Wuhan, and Hefei. We find that house prices, the floor area of new homes sold, and existing-home transaction volumes have all shown signs of stabilizing in these cities. House prices have even risen modestly in a few core cities. By contrast, real estate markets in most third- and fourth-tier cities remain weak. In other words, stabilization is concentrated in core cities rather than broad-based, which is why we refer to it as “structural stabilization.”
Thus, for the 33 core cities, if new starts continue to decline sharply, excess housing inventory could be rapidly reduced, potentially giving way to a shortage. This would provide additional support for house prices and demand and could accelerate the housing market’s recovery.
Over the past few years, the deep adjustment in the real estate market has been the main driver of the widening current account surplus. The underlying mechanism is that the real estate downturn led to a sharp decline in the investment rate, while the saving rate adjusted with a lag. The resulting widening of the saving–investment gap translated directly into a larger current account surplus.
As the real estate market gradually stabilizes, the drag from real estate investment will diminish, while household precautionary saving will stop rising. The saving–investment gap will therefore narrow, and the current account surplus will stabilize at a high level rather than continue to widen. This process bears some resemblance to the decline in China’s current account surplus after 2008, when the RMB 4 trillion stimulus package drove a sharp expansion in domestic investment, significantly narrowing the saving–investment gap.
By contrast, the stabilization of the manufacturing capacity cycle since 2024 has clearly not relied on comparable demand-side stimulus. Instead, the sequence has been “supply adjustment first, followed by a moderate recovery in demand”: a market-driven process in which firms voluntarily slowed investment and retired inefficient capacity in response to weak demand. This differs fundamentally from the post-2016 cyclical reversal driven by a sharp rebound in demand.
According to CF40 research, the new economy’s total value added rose from about 6.1% of GDP in 2018 to 10.4% in 2025, while the corresponding share for real estate fell from 12.7% to 8.4%. By 2025, the new economy’s total value-added share had surpassed that of real estate and had become an important component of GDP.
A defining characteristic of new-economy firms is their greater emphasis on R&D and their ability to generate more operating revenue and profits with less debt. In 2025, new-economy firms accounted for only 11.9% of the total interest-bearing debt of firms in the full sample, compared with 17.8% of total operating revenue and 29.5% of total net profits across the sample. Their share of total R&D expenditure was even higher, at 47.6%. As the new economy accounts for a growing share of China’s economy, the country’s growth model will gradually evolve.
The negative wealth effect of the real estate adjustment is fading, but households’ propensity to consume remains well below its pre-pandemic level, while further improvements in social security and public services are constrained by fiscal pressures. Rather than rising sharply, the consumption rate is therefore more likely to stabilize as the drag from real estate fades. If supportive policies are fully implemented, the consumption rate could gradually rise.
Moreover, the more advanced a manufacturing industry, the lower the share of output going to compensation of employees tends to be. For example, compensation of employees accounts for only 7.8% and 7.6% of gross output in electrical machinery and equipment manufacturing and automobile manufacturing, respectively—two industries that together encompass the “new three.” The corresponding share is 8.7% in computer, communications, and other electronic equipment manufacturing, the industry most closely associated with AI.
On a value-added basis, compensation of employees accounts for 36%, 42%, and 47% in these three industries, respectively, all below the service-sector average. This means that even if the new economy continues to expand rapidly and drive economic growth, households’ share of income in primary distribution will not automatically increase and could even decline. This is because these new-economy industries allocate a smaller share of their output to compensation of employees than the current economy-wide average.
On monetary policy, emphasis should move further away from pursuing credit-volume expansion toward lowering interest rates, improving inflation expectations, and restoring nominal demand. Real estate no longer performs its previous role in credit expansion, while the new economy is relatively less dependent on bank credit. Growth in bank lending and total social financing is therefore increasingly difficult to use on its own as a measure of whether monetary policy is sufficiently accommodative.
One possible aggregate benchmark is that “nominal growth in broad fiscal expenditure should exceed nominal GDP growth.” At present, local governments face multiple constraints, including declining land-related revenues, debt resolution efforts, and rising mandatory spending commitments. Near-term fiscal expansion will therefore need to rely more heavily on the central government.
The new economy has demonstrated China’s capacity to create new productive capacity, but the more important issue for the next stage is how to translate that capacity into household income and final consumption. New-economy firms have high R&D spending, high productivity, and low reliance on debt—an important direction for economic transformation. However, if the industrial structure merely shifts from traditional manufacturing toward more advanced manufacturing, higher productivity will not necessarily translate automatically into a larger household income share or a higher consumption rate.

articles.title_orig: Yemen’s Houthis Take Second Swipe at Tallest Tower in Saudi Capital
articles.title_zh: Yemen’s Houthis Take Second Swipe at Tallest Tower in Saudi Capital
articles.content_orig:
Saudi Arabia and Bahrain reported attacks by Iran-linked forces over the weekend, as Iran's foreign minister said his government remains open to a deal to end the war with the U.S.
"Intercepted and destroyed a drone launched by the Houthi terrorist militia toward the Riyadh area," the Saudi-led Coalition to Support Legitimacy in Yemen, which has been leading the fight against the Iran-backed group, said Sunday in a post on X.
The coalition said late Saturday that its air defenses "intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile" launched by the Yemen-based Houthis toward Saudi Arabia's western region, which includes some of the country's sensitive energy refining and export infrastructure.
Neighboring Bahrain also said it came under Iranian fire.
"As a result of the heinous Iranian aggression, a civilian industrial facility was targeted, causing a fire at the site," Bahrain's Ministry of Interior said on X. The ministry later said two people , a Bahraini citizen and a Pakistani resident, were injured in the attack.
Bahrain is home to the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet.
Iranian state media reported late Saturday that the country's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps fired missiles and drones at U.S. military facilities in Bahrain .
A separate Iranian media report claimed the IRGC's air defenses intercepted and destroyed a U.S. MQ-9 drone .
U.S. Central Command did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on either Iranian report.
Meanwhile, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said his government remains open to a negotiated settlement to the war. An agreement aimed at developing a permanent peace deal signed in June between President Donald Trump and his Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian — the so-called Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding — later broke down.
"The Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding is no longer on the table and has no implementation relevance," Araghchi told the Iran newspaper.
"However, the commitments that the U.S. had accepted in that Memorandum of Understanding and the principle that the implementation of those commitments can pave the way for reaching a final agreement are still accepted by both sides," he said.
The war, which began with U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on Iranian targets on Feb. 28, has resulted in major disruptions to energy shipments through the Strait of Hormuz between Iran and Oman.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations reported that two tankers near Oman were struck by unidentified projectiles on Saturday.
Iran has imposed curbs on vessels moving through the strait, a major sticking point in negotiations with the U.S.
Oil prices have fallen for three straight weeks, however, as traders weighed strong Middle East flows and rising U.S. inventories.
International benchmark Brent crude fell 3.4% for the week, while U.S. crude tumbled 5.2%.

articles.title_orig: Israeli air strike kills Hamas internal security chief in Gaza
articles.title_zh: Israeli air strike kills Hamas internal security chief in Gaza
articles.content_orig:
At least seven Palestinians, including a senior Hamas security official, have been killed in Israeli air strikes in the Gaza Strip, health officials and first responders say.
Naeem Abu Nahel, the head of Hamas's internal security service, was targeted in western Gaza City, Gaza's Hamas-run interior ministry said. The 50-year-old had only been in the position since September, when his predecessor was captured in a raid by Israeli special forces .
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz announced that Abu Nahel was "eliminated" by the Israeli military.
The six other people were killed in two earlier air strikes elsewhere in Gaza.
Three people, including a teenage boy, were killed in the Wadi Gaza area, south of Gaza City, according to the health officials and first responders. The other three were killed at a police station in the al-Mawasi area, west of Khan Younis, they added.
Gaza's police force, which operates under the interior ministry, said two of its officers were among those who died in the second attack. It also accused Israel of "an ongoing campaign targeting the police apparatus aimed at sowing chaos" in the territory.
The Israeli military said it struck "military operatives" in both areas.
Witnesses said an Israeli drone targeted Naeem Abu Nahel as he was walking on a side street near a tent camp for displaced people in Gaza City.
Several other people were reportedly seriously injured in the strike.
The Israeli military said Abu Nahel had "possessed extensive institutional knowledge" about Hamas's internal security service - which is responsible for enforcing discipline, protecting infrastructure and rooting out informants - and that his death constituted "a blow to the apparatus's management capabilities".
It also alleged that he had advanced attacks on Israeli troops and civilians during the war and that it killed him "to remove the threat he posed".
Gaza's interior ministry said Abu Nahel's killing followed what it described as the internal security service's "important achievements in combating gangs collaborating with the occupation [Israel] and operating in areas under the control of its military".
Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under Hamas's control, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.
At least 1,679 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.
The humanitarian situation also remains dire, with heavy rainfall earlier this month causing flooding and damage to thousands of shelters for displaced families.
The UN and its partners have called on Israel - which controls Gaza's crossings - to allow in more supplies to help Palestinians prepare for the winter, including tents, heaters and water pumps, as well as vaccines and medicines to combat infectious diseases.
On Tuesday, the health ministry warned that there had been a rapid rise in cases of meningitis, with 272 reported in October - about eight times the usual monthly average.
Fifteen deaths had been attributed to the infection so far this year, including five reported between August and October, it said.
Israeli military body Cogat said on Monday it was "working to provide a dedicated humanitarian response" and that a newly approved package of pumps, generators, water tankers and medical equipment had been presented at a meeting with UN agencies.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,740 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

articles.title_zh: Micron Stock Is Counting on a Buyback Bounce. Why It’s No Slam Dunk.
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
When it comes to the AI trade, this has been the year of AMD ( AMD ). AMD's stock has sizzled, up 112% year to date compared to an 11.5% drop for its top rival Nvidia.
As Nvidia's ( NVDA ) founder Jensen Huang has been embroiled in scandal and the tech trade has been pressured, AMD shares have hung tough. The stock is down 12.2% over the past month versus a 22% decline for Nvidia.
The biggest question for AMD right now is this: Does Huang's stunning return as CEO of Nvidia mean bad news for AMD in 2027 and beyond?
Pros think AMD will be just fine, for now.
"I don't see how this changes it completely," Moor Insights & Strategy founder Patrick Moorhead said on Sozzi Unleashed . "I was saying early on when Jensen left that nothing changes for 18 months. And the reason is the supply chain is locked, the wafers are locked, data center configurations are locked around Nvidia design. So nothing would change, I think, if Jensen had been removed permanently."
Shares of Nvidia fell 5% in premarket trading on Tuesday after a 31.2% surge on news that founder Jensen Huang had been reinstated as CEO. That came just 12 days after he resigned amid a personal scandal and federal chip-export probes.
Interestingly, AMD shares rose 6.3% yesterday — a telling move that investors continue to believe in the AMD story.
It's a good story to buy into.
CEO Lisa Su — Yahoo Finance's 2026 CEO of the Year award winner — surprised everyone by spending $8.2 billion to scoop up World Labs , gaining a true AI innovator that focuses on software for 3D environments.
World Labs was founded in 2024 and is led by Fei-Fei Li, a leading AI researcher known in tech circles as the "Godmother of AI." She was once the chief scientist at Google Cloud ( GOOG ).
Just a few weeks ago, AMD delivered a strong double beat in its third quarter earnings report. Third quarter sales jumped 45% year over year to a record $13.38 billion, comfortably surpassing Wall Street consensus estimates of roughly $13.06 billion.
Adjusted earnings climbed 74% to $2.09 per share, easily topping analyst projections of $1.94 per share.
The blowout performance was anchored by AMD's Data Center segment, where revenue surged 97% to a record $8.5 billion on robust demand for EPYC server processors and the production ramp of Instinct MI450 AI accelerators.
For the fourth quarter, AMD said it sees 50% sequential growth in data centers. In 2027, Su guided to revenue growing more than 80%, with server revenue doubling and data center AI more than doubling.
Amid a year of impressive earnings execution, AMD also unveiled its next-generation AI chips, headlined by the Instinct MI450 Series GPUs and the 6th Gen EPYC Venice CPUs. The new chips are designed to power AMD's new Helios rack-scale AI systems , which combine GPUs, CPUs, networking, and software into an integrated platform for training and running large AI models.
Microsoft ( MSFT ) said it began deploying Helios across Azure AI services in the second half of 2026.
The company also announced a major tie-up with Anthropic ( ANT ), significantly expanding its push to challenge Nvidia in the AI infrastructure market.
Anthropic plans to deploy up to 2 gigawatts of the Instinct MI450 GPUs in its Helios system beginning in the first half of 2027 — a deal that could be worth tens of billions of dollars over time. AMD also committed to invest up to $5 billion in Anthropic, marking one of the chipmaker's largest strategic investments ever.
The biggest thing to watch, experts say, is how a hungry-to-prove-himself Huang executes on new chip designs over the next five to seven years. If Huang unlocks an epic gear on the design front, then the entire chip space could be in trouble from a market share perspective.
"Jensen will be on a mission," EMJ Capital founder Eric Jackson said on Sozzi Unleashed .
For now, though, AMD is still in the AI game in a big way.

articles.title_orig: Zelenskiy confirms Ukraine hit Russian ship in Gulf of Finland, ally Norway urges caution
articles.title_zh: Zelenskiy confirms Ukraine hit Russian ship in Gulf of Finland, ally Norway urges caution
articles.content_orig:
A Russian cargo ship struck by drones in the Gulf of Finland has left Finnish territorial waters after posing a “serious danger” there, according to Finland’s President Alexander Stubb.
Stubb said late on Sunday that Finland would continue working to maintain stability and security in the Gulf of Finland and thanked the authorities for their response to Saturday’s incident.
Finland’s military said the strike on the Sparta II on Saturday was likely carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it was previously anchored. The 16 crew members were evacuated onto a nearby Russian ship.
A fire aboard the Sparta II continued to burn through the night despite efforts to extinguish it, the Finnish coastguard said.
“Unfortunately, the consequences of Russia’s war of aggression are also visible in our region,” Stubb said on X.
Pictures and video released by the coastguard on Sunday showed several vessels spraying the Sparta II with water cannon overnight to put out the flames and cool down containers stacked on its deck.
Ukraine has sent waves of military drones towards Russia’s northwestern coastal region of Leningrad this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling onto NATO territory.
The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, was damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland Island, the Finnish Defence Forces said, corroborating an account by Russian officials.
Finland’s Prime Minister Petteri Orpo suggested the incident was related to Russia’s war on Ukraine.
“War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity … Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor,” Orpo said on X.
The risk of further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, cannot be ruled out, Estonian Navy Commander Ivo Vark told public broadcaster ERR on Sunday.
Finland’s military said last week that it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks.
The Sparta II is a 121-metre (397-foot) Russian-flagged cargo vessel owned by Russian shipping company Oboronlogistika that left St Petersburg on Friday, according to data from the London Stock Exchange.
The vessel is subject to United States sanctions, according to the US Department of the Treasury.
Oboronlogistika provides logistics services for the Russian Ministry of Defence, according to the company’s website.

articles.title_orig: iOS 27 adds new Messages app setting I instantly started using
articles.title_zh: iOS 27 adds new Messages app setting I instantly started using
articles.content_orig:
iOS 27 brought several new features to the Messages app, including a setting that’s long been a popular request: the ability to customize or turn off the audio button. Here’s how to use it.
With iOS 27, Apple fixed a lot of bugs and also granted many feature requests from over the years.
Siri AI is the biggest example of that, offering a big upgrade over the old Siri. But smaller changes in apps like Calendar , Mail , and Messages reflect this focus on wish fulfillment.
In Messages, there’s a new setting that I instantly starting using. It lets you turn off the audio button that normally lives on the right side of the text input field.
The audio button has been conveniently accessible there for years, but I never use it. I don’t think I’ve ever sent an audio message. Sometimes I use dictation, but that’s always available from the bottom-right of the keyboard.
Since I never need that button, the only time it gets pressed is by accident. And as I suspect a lot of users have encountered— including Justin Bieber —it’s very easy to hit by accident.
Thankfully, iOS 27 has the fix. To disable the audio button, follow these steps:
Even if you turn the audio button off, you can still send audio messages by hitting the + button to open your iMessage apps then selecting ‘Audio.’
If you prefer to keep the button active, you can alternately now select ‘Record Audio’ or ‘Start Dictation’ as its function. That way the button will always stay set to your preference instead of dynamically changing like it did before.
Will you disable the audio button in Messages? Let us know in the comments.
FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More.
Check out 9to5Mac on YouTube for more Apple news:
Ryan got his start in journalism as an Editor at MacStories, where he worked for four years covering Apple news, writing app reviews, and more. For two years he co-hosted the Adapt podcast on Relay FM, which focused entirely on the iPad. As a result, it should come as no surprise that his favorite Apple device is the iPad Pro.

articles.title_orig: Gisèle Pelicot to sue publisher that sent nude images to media, says she's "once again humiliated"
articles.title_zh: Gisèle Pelicot to sue publisher that sent nude images to media, says she's "once again humiliated"
articles.content_orig:
Gisèle Pelicot, the French woman who spoke out about being drugged and raped by her husband and dozens of other men, said Monday that she had been "once again humiliated" after nude photos and videos of her were sent to media outlets to promote a book that she said is dismissive of her husband's crimes.
Pelicot, 73, told France's BFMTV that she will take legal action against the publisher, Tinard, and the author of the book, French psychoanalyst Sabine Prokhoris.
The book criticizes the concept of coercive control and questions whether Pelicot was really a victim, suggesting she could have been complicit in her husband's actions despite her having been surreptitiously drugged for years.
"I am deeply shocked that images relating to my most intimate life could be exhibited and exploited for commercial purposes," Pelicot said in a statement to the French broadcaster, adding: "Above all, I refuse to have my story rewritten by implying that I was complicit in what I suffered."
"Today, I find myself humiliated, exposed, and hurt once again. As if the ordeal of the trial wasn't enough," she said. "I fought to regain my dignity and my freedom. I will not let anyone take them away from me."
Pelicot became a global symbol of resilience in 2024 when she waived her right to anonymity in her then-husband Dominique's trial. He was convicted and sentenced to 20 years in prison for his abuse — and for inviting 50 other men to join him in raping his wife while she was incapacitated repeatedly over the course of a decade.
"How can you imagine that your husband is drugging you? It's unthinkable — impossible," she told CBS News in February. "In fact, I was manipulated for about 10 years. Because he was looking me in the eyes every day while knowing he was poisoning me. But I never saw that. I saw a kind, caring man."
She said she waived her anonymity during the trial to show that "shame has to change sides," from victims to perpetrators.
On its website, the publisher Tinard said it had offered "our sincerest apologies" to Pelicot and that it would not be reprinting the book after 280 copies already printed are sold. It said "no images of rape or pornographic videos were leaked to the press."
It is not clear where the publisher got the nude images of Pelicot. In her statements to French media, Pelicot did not question their authenticity. She also did not confirm or deny a report by the French weekly news outlet Le Canard Enchaîne, which said the images were among those taken by her former husband and presented during his trial as evidence.
Prokhoris, the author, said she had given "full responsibility" for the promotional campaign to the publisher, according to French news agency AFP.
AFP said the back-cover blurb on the book asks readers to "think freely" about the notion of coercive control, which Prokhoris describes as "a cornerstone of #MeToo orthodoxy" that is "fundamentally ambiguous" and, she says, involves "each of the parties in an equally responsible, though not symmetrical, way."
"There are two types of violence that have been committed," Pelicot's lawyer Christophe Bigot told BFM. "There is, on the one hand, the fact that intimate images of her were sent without her consent in the context of purely commercial communication, and then there is a book that calls into question her status as a victim."
"It is a clear violation of the law, and she does not intend to let it go unchallenged," he said.

articles.title_orig: China probes Shanghai party boss Chen Jining, marking fourth Politburo member to fall since 2025
articles.title_zh: China probes Shanghai party boss Chen Jining, marking fourth Politburo member to fall since 2025
articles.content_orig:
The Communist Party chief of Shanghai, considered one of the potential heirs to Chinese leader Xi Jinping, has suddenly been placed under investigation –– marking an escalation of an anti-corruption purge that’s already ensnared a large swath of the country’s top talent .
Chen Jining, 62, who has run China’s largest city and financial center since October 2022, is facing a corruption charge and is suspected of “serious violations of discipline,” state media Xinhua said on Tuesday evening.
It is a stunning downfall for Chen, who was seen as a rising political star and even being mentioned among potential successors to longtime leader Xi by China watchers.
Xi, who is all but certain to assume a precedent-breaking fourth term in office next year, has executed an unrelenting anti-corruption drive for well over a decade that has brought down senior political, military and judiciary figures once thought untouchable. The speed and scale that effort has reached unseen levels in recent months.
Chen becomes the fourth of the 24 member politburo –– the top-echelon of power in China –– to fall since the last party congress in 2022.
The investigation is being conducted by China’s main anti-corruption body, the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection.
Chen’s last public appearance appears to be Thursday, November 19, when he inspected the headquarters of a Chinese shipping conglomerate.
Unsurprisingly, government platforms in Shanghai have quickly taken down posts mentioning Chen.
Trained as an environmental scientist, the urbane and English-speaking Chen rose through the party ranks in the past two decades. Before moving to Shanghai, he was mayor of Beijing and orchestrated the 2022 Winter Olympics Games in the capital.
His appointment to the top party job in Shanghai marked a quick elevation. The post usually paves the way for further promotion to the Politburo Standing Committee - the pinnacle of the party’s power structure. Both Xi and China’s former leader Jiang Zemin have followed this path.
It can be lonely at the top. And that’s just how China’s leader likes it
Prior to his Beijing mayorship, Chen spent over a decade at the Ministry of Environment and Ecology. He also served as the president of the Tsinghua University in Beijing, one of China’s most prestigious academic institutions.
After earning a master’s degree in civil and environmental engineering from Tsinghua in 1980s, Chen went to study at London’s Imperial College, where he earned a doctorate degree.
Just in the past two month, Xi’s clampdown of top officials saw the downfall of Beijing’s deputy mayor and a retired former mayor of Chongqing who had withstood several prior political storms.
The party’s top military decision-making body, the usually seven-member Central Military Commission, is now down to only two members with one of those being Xi himself .
Since Xi, 73, came to power over 14 years ago millions of rank-and-file officials have also been  caught in his dragnet.
Between 2012 and 2022, over 500 ministerial-level officials were convicted, removed from their posts, and expelled from the party for corruption, according to official data from the party’s Central Commission of Discipline Inspection (CCDI) – with more than 410 officials purged in the last three years alone.

articles.title_orig: Congress to grill Jensen Huang over ties with China and Trump’s intervention
articles.title_zh: Congress to grill Jensen Huang over ties with China and Trump’s intervention
articles.content_orig:
Republican pushback to Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO is growing, despite President Donald Trump earlier downplaying any blowback from his party.
The chairs of the GOP-led House intelligence and foreign affairs committees as well as the House select committee on the Chinese Communist Party criticized Nvidia in a joint statement on Monday. Reps. Rick Crawford, Brian Mast and John Moolenaar said the company’s “brief internal investigation” and reinstatement of Huang “do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed.”
GOP Rep. Pat Harrigan of North Carolina also blasted Huang’s reinstatement as a “mistake.”
Is Nvidia’s CEO too big to fail?
“Today, we sent a signal that one man’s financial impact on our economy outweighs the importance of good governance, good citizenship, and adherence to the law,” the North Carolina Republican wrote in a post on X . “That is a dangerous precedent to set, and one I believe will come at a significant cost to our country in the long run.”
GOP Sen. Kevin Cramer of North Dakota wrote , “The legal and reputational risk of hiring a CEO who may very well be convicted in the United States or other nations of violating espionage and export control laws is now born by the board of Nvidia, but the national security risk is passed along to the United States military and its citizens.”
Sen. John Curtis of Utah went as far as to scrutinize the input Nvidia said it received from “senior levels of the United States government” that Huang poses no national security risk.
“Nvidia’s board says it relied on input from senior U.S. officials to conclude that bringing Jensen Huang back posed no national security risk. I have some questions. Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?” Curtis said .
Arkansas GOP Sen. Tom Cotton, who is known as a China hawk, said in a post on X that Congress must investigate further and called for his chip export bill to pass.
“The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it’s not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back,” said Cotton, who is the outgoing Senate Intelligence Committee chairman. “Congress has much to investigate and we will pass overwhelmingly bipartisan chip export-control bills, including my Chip Security Act, one way or the other.”
That legislation proposes requiring some kind of “location verification mechanism” on advanced chips and directs the Commerce Department to study “other potential chip security mechanisms.”
Attorney General Todd Blanche on Monday evening, however, refused to answer during an interview with Fox News whether Huang had been cleared of any national security concerns or potential legal violations before being reinstated.
CNN reported earlier Monday that several other Republicans have criticized or questioned the move to reinstate Huang — including Sens. John Cornyn and Pete Ricketts and Rep. Don Bacon.
Earlier Monday in an interview with CNBC, Trump dismissed any concerns from GOP lawmakers saying, “When I speak to them, they’re going to be great.”
This story has been updated with additional information.

articles.title_orig: Snowden on steroids: AI agents in phones trigger surveillance fears
articles.title_zh: Snowden on steroids: AI agents in phones trigger surveillance fears
articles.content_orig:
AI agents are lurking in your phone, hoovering up your messages, pictures and emails in a privacy breach that "makes the Edward Snowden revelations look like a joke," privacy proponents are warning.
Privacy-preserving messaging app Signal has started blocking screenshots by default in an attempt to stop AI agents from reading people's screens and capturing potentially sensitive data.
The makers behind Signal — which is considered the industry gold standard for confidential, encrypted messaging — warned that Google, Apple and Microsoft are integrating autonomous agents "deep" within their device operating systems, allowing the agents to bypass privacy safeguards in individual apps.
"The ability for billions of devices to permanently spy on their users makes the Edward Snowden revelations look like a joke," Udbhav Tiwari, head of strategy and global affairs at Signal, told POLITICO, referring to the 2013 disclosures about mass U.S. government surveillance.
Tiwari warned that governments with a penchant for surveillance could ask tech firms for access to data gathered by AI agents, skipping the need to break end-to-end encryption or install malware on someone’s device.
Apple, Google and Microsoft declined to comment on Signal’s claims.
Itxaso Domínguez de Olazábal, policy adviser at European digital rights group EDRi, called for "serious limits" on what AI agents can access. "There is something deeply worrying about a not-so-far-away future where the companies controlling our operating systems can effectively decide how much privacy we are allowed to have, even when we deliberately choose services designed to protect it," she said.
"Probably the most sensitive device in your entire life is your phone. If it gets nicked, the person stealing your phone is not going to have access to your whole life. We're undoing all those safeguards by inviting AI agents onto these devices," said Gus Hosein, executive director of privacy NGO Privacy International.
Signal is pushing for makers of operating systems to provide tools so apps can opt out of AI data access and processing.
Operating system level AI agents have already launched in many countries globally, but rollout is slower in the EU. Apple has cited the EU’s digital competition rulebook as a key hurdle for the rollout of its latest AI virtual assistant features.
Social media giant Meta is also rolling out its own AI agent, Muse, which launched in the United Kingdom on Tuesday . Digital regulators including the Information Commissioner's Office already warned last month that AI agent products “may amplify and accelerate risks” to consumers. The British privacy authority said this week that Meta committed to a “voluntary monitoring and reporting scheme” to enable ongoing scrutiny, and that it is preparing new guidance on how privacy law applies to AI agents.
Meta has said its new AI agent is “private, safe and secure by design," and that it has "engaged constructively" with regulators.
Beyond the most high-risk situations, there are concerns AI agents could also gather data to repurpose for things like AI training or targeted advertising.
Ireland’s powerful privacy regulator, which oversees data protection policies at Apple, Google, Meta, Microsoft and other tech giants, is also cracking down on how "third-party" data is hoovered up by AI agents and repurposed.
Third-party data pertains to someone who isn't directly dealing with the AI agent; for example, you send a message or holiday pictures to a friend without knowing they've given an AI agent permission to access their messages.
The Irish Data Protection Commission intervened in the past month to stop Elon Musk-owned X from feeding AI models with third party data collected by its Grok Bot, POLITICO first reported .
Irish Data Protection Commissioner Niamh Sweeney said last week that it is "much more challenging" to inform third parties about their data being processed, or give them a chance to opt out, when they have “no idea” that their data could also be scooped up.
