articles.title_orig: Who really owns the land in Albania that Jared Kushner wants to develop?
articles.title_zh: Who really owns the land in Albania that Jared Kushner wants to develop?
articles.content_orig:
The sun sets over coastal mountains near the city of Vlore, the region where Jared Kushner plans to build a five-star luxury resort. The land that Kushner bought for this project, though, is claimed by several local Albanians and its ownership is being investigated by state prosecutors. Rob Schmitz/NPR hide caption
ZVERNEC, Albania — In the summer of 2021, Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump boarded a yacht owned by Nat Rothschild, an heir to the European banking family.  On the way from Montenegro to Greece, the yacht anchored off the coast of Albania.
And, as Kushner told an investment conference last year, that's when Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama arrived at the boat to tell them about his plan for the country.
"I was very impressed by what he wanted to do with the country," said Kushner. "I really didn't know anything about the country and I didn't understand the history, and the darkness of the history with the communism and terrible leadership led to it being fully undeveloped as a nation."
A year later, Kushner was looking for development opportunities in the Balkans. He returned to the Albanian coast — to the city of Vlore, which was finishing the construction of an airport atop a wetland near an undeveloped coastline. "And obviously, a country's going to build an airport by the coast in a place they think is most beautiful," Kushner told the conference, "so we went there and we were looking for opportunities, and we found some incredible opportunities."
Kushner found those opportunities at Hidrovor Beach, an expanse of caramel-colored sand along the southern Albanian coast, with the gentle waves of the Adriatic lapping its perimeter and a view of an uninhabited island. A company working for Kushner purchased this land and 300 acres surrounding it for more than $130 million in April. But several people here tell NPR this is not Kushner's land.
Gentian Mocka says his family has owned this strip of beach, named Hidrovor Beach, since the time of the Ottoman Empire. The land is now slated to be developed for a luxury hotel owned by Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump. In the background is Sazan Island, a publicly owned island that Trump and Kushner also say they will develop. Rob Schmitz/NPR hide caption
"This land here belonged to my family for centuries," says Gentian Mocka, who claims his family has owned this strip of beach and wetland since the time of the Ottoman Empire. He provided NPR land titles that appear to prove this.
After World War II, Albania's Communist government seized it — along with all private land.
When communism fell in 1991, families like Mocka's embarked on a years-long process to get their land back. "But then our problems started with the guys that were much more powerful than we were — had a lot of political support, were very rich and very well connected with the politics of that time," says Mocka.
In 2005, Mocka learned that someone else was laying claim to his family's land — a fellow Albanian named Artur Shehu. It was a familiar name for those who lived here in the 1990s, when the regional capital of Vlore was outside the control of the country's government. It was instead run by mafia-style gangs. At the time, Shehu was well-known to police in Vlore for his alleged involvement in a crime syndicate that, according to Albanian prosecutors, smuggled drugs and migrants into Europe. He fled Albania in 1999, after what police say was a shootout with a rival gang.
He ended up in the United States, where he received asylum in 2001 and, later, became a U.S. citizen. The 60-year-old Shehu now lives in a villa in Miami Beach. But he's continued to manage a growing real estate portfolio back in Albania through an associate in Vlore named Pellumb Petritaj.
The pair has claimed plots of land — including Mocka's family plot — up and down the southern Albanian coast, and prosecutors have taken notice. In 2018, Petritaj served three years in prison for forging land titles on behalf of Shehu. And on Nov. 18, Petritaj was sentenced to another seven years in prison for falsifying documents to $17 million worth of oceanfront property in the city of Vlore on behalf of Shehu. The court ordered the land — which does not include Mocka's family plot — confiscated from Shehu last week. The pair has also claimed oceanfront farmland in the village of Zvernec, adjacent to Mocka's land.
The pair has also claimed oceanfront farmland in the village of Zvernec, adjacent to Mocka's land.
The quiet village has only a couple hundred residents. Most of them, like Minella Konomi and Natasha Kota, are past the age of 70. On a recent warm and sunny afternoon, the two are resting on benches in the courtyard of the village church after a day of harvesting olives. They nod their heads when asked about Artur Shehu.
"He is from the village of Kanina, far from here and up in the mountains," says Konomi, motioning inland, "but his family has never lived here. He's involved in shady dealings."
The village of Zvernec, along the Adriatic coast, is at the center of a land dispute involving Jared Kushner. Several of the village's residents say the land that Kushner is claiming is actually theirs. Rob Schmitz/NPR hide caption
Then Kota speaks up. "There wasn't a single soul of that family living here, going back to the Ottoman times," she says. "But we've heard stories about him, and we're very scared of him."
Twenty years ago, Kota, Konomi and dozens of others in this village learned that Artur Shehu had somehow acquired their farmland. They filed suit in Albanian court to reclaim their land, a fight that escalated this past April when Shehu sold the 300-acre parcel that includes what they say is their farmland to a company developing a luxury resort project for Kushner.
That transaction, however, is under review.
In court documents obtained by NPR, Albanian prosecutors argue that the land involved in Kushner's development is "suspected of having been illegally acquired through forgery."
A spokesman for Kushner did not respond to NPR's request for comment by the time this article was published. Kushner had previously issued a statement on his website saying his partnership purchased the land from a private party in a private transaction. "Title was reviewed by counsel and verified," the statement says.
Shehu did not respond to NPR's request for comment. He has previously denied any wrongdoing. However, in Tirana, a former lawyer for Shehu was willing to talk.
"The people that Artur [Shehu] has authorized by power of attorney to deal with his family's properties committed a forgery in which they removed the property from the brother of Artur's grandfather and passed it to Artur's grandfather," says Kujtim Cakrani. "That is the whole story of the property."
Cakrani says Shehu's associates forged an inheritance certificate that made it appear that Shehu's grandfather had owned the land, which was then passed to Artur Shehu himself. And then last April, Shehu sold that land to Moutaz and Ramez Al-Khayyat, Syrian-born Qatari billionaire brothers who are financial partners of Jared Kushner.
Cakrani says that when he discovered that Artur Shehu was involved in this alleged forgery, he dropped him as his client. "I could no longer continue representing him because of the seriousness of the matter," he says. "It is impossible for me, with these documents that he has, to defend him."
And this is why, Cakrani says, Albanian state prosecutors have put Shehu under investigation and froze his bank accounts. Cakrani says he is now representing a group of 30 relatives of Shehu who he claims to be the rightful owners of this land.
Kujtim Cakrani is the former lawyer of Artur Shehu, the man who sold the property along Albania's southern coast to a pair of billionaire brothers who represent Jared Kushner. He says he's since dropped Shehu as a client. Rob Schmitz/NPR hide caption
Gentian Mocka, as well as Minella Konomi and Natasha Kota in Zvernec, tell NPR that nobody by the name of Shehu

articles.title_orig: Ukraine insists attack on Russian ships in Libya was self-defence
articles.title_zh: Ukraine insists attack on Russian ships in Libya was self-defence
articles.content_orig:
Some NATO countries are voicing increasing anxiety as hostilities in the nearly five-year war sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine spread beyond the two countries' borders.
Polish authorities accused Russia again Tuesday of deliberately violating the nation's airspace as officials said a surveillance drone briefly crossed the Polish border before turning back into Ukraine. Poland, a member of the U.S.-led NATO alliance and a neighbor and close ally of Ukraine, accused Moscow of a deliberate provocation late last week after three Russian missiles landed on Polish soil.
Polish Deputy Defense Minister Paweł Zalewski said in a radio interview on Tuesday that the Russian drone crossed the border for a "very short time" and was "monitored from the very beginning."
"I spoke with the Operational Command of the Armed Forces, and the decision was made not to shoot it down, as they did not want to risk any casualties or damage on the civilian side," Zalewski told Radio Poland. "We assume this was an intentional act."
Norway's Defense Minister Tore Sandvik said Tuesday, meanwhile, that the Scandinavian country was speaking with Ukrainian officials about the "need for stability in our near areas," following a strike on Saturday that hit a U.S.-sanctioned Russian cargo ship in international waters in the Gulf of Finland.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy acknowledged Ukraine had carried out that strike in a social media post on Monday, saying the country's forces used seven domestically produced naval drones to attack the ship.
The Sparta II cargo vessel, which is operated by Russian defense logistics firm Oboronlogistika, has been under U.S. sanctions since 2022 for illicit transportation of military hardware. Russian authorities confirmed that it had been towed back to a Russian port on Tuesday.
Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani spoke Tuesday with his Ukrainian counterpart Andriy Sybiha, meanwhile, in a phone call to express Italy's concern over another Ukrainian attack carried out over the weekend, this one off the coast of Libya.
Zelenskyy lauded Ukrainian forces on Monday for that attack, which sank a Russian warship and damaged another U.S.-sanctioned Russian cargo vessel, the MV Angara, off the North African nation's Mediterranean coast, where Russia has a naval base.
"The minister emphasized to his Ukrainian counterpart how crucial it is for Italy to keep working to prevent the conflict with Russia from spreading into the Mediterranean," Italy's Foreign Ministry said Tuesday in a readout of the ministers' call.
Zelenskyy framed the strikes on the Russian ships as legitimate defensive actions in response to Russia's ongoing deadly missile and drone strikes, which it launches from land, sea and air.
"Despite all the enemy's efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk," Zelenskyy said. "We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia's aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons."
The Russian Foreign Ministry this week accused Estonia, another NATO ally, of being "on the verge of triggering open war" after the small Baltic country announced it would close its land border with Russia starting Dec. 1.
Estonia accused Russian intelligence agencies last week of a plot to infiltrate and sabotage the domestic defense company Threod Systems.
"Any attempt to threaten Estonia's security, sow fear, or act hostilely against us will be met with a decisive response," Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said in a statement last week. "By closing the border crossings, we are sending a clear message to the Kremlin: Russia's hostile actions come at a cost. The more aggressively Russia behaves, the narrower its room for manoeuvre becomes."
The Estonian move came only a couple of weeks after Poland's prime minister said a large-scale security operation launched along the Polish-Russian border may have prevented a sabotage or provocation operation by Russian operatives.
While NATO members' concern over the spread of the war has been more clearly iterated in recent weeks, Ben Hodges, a former top commander of the U.S. Army in Europe, told CBS News on Tuesday that, in his opinion, all of Ukraine's actions constitute a legitimate defense in the face of Russia's aggression.
"Ukraine is doing exactly what they need to do to disrupt Russian oil/gas exports and other international activities to degrade Russia's ability to sustain its war effort," Hodges said. "This is also an important signal to anyone who would willingly support Russia's shadow fleet ."
Moscow uses its so-called shadow fleet —   hundreds of dubiously registered tankers — to evade international sanctions on its oil sales, keeping money flowing in to power its war machine.
Hodges told CBS News that Kyiv has likely calculated the risks involved in attacking Russian vessels in neutral waters.
"The risk is that Russia will attempt to use these as an excuse for its attacks against the Ukrainian economy and civilian infrastructure," he told CBS News. "But Ukraine knows this and anticipates it."
"Most European countries also already understand this and will not be moved by it," he added.

articles.title_orig: China unveils new space mission crew, with a Pakistani astronaut set to board its space station
articles.title_zh: China unveils new space mission crew, with a Pakistani astronaut set to board its space station
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
China has announced the crew for the upcoming space launch to its Tiangong space station , including a Pakistani astronaut, who will be the first foreigner to board the orbiting outpost.
Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, who served as a pilot in the Pakistan Air Force, will board China’s Shenzhou 24 spacecraft powered by the Long March 2F rocket along with Chinese colleagues Tang Hongbo and Wu Yi, the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) announced on Tuesday.
The trio is scheduled to launch from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre in northwest China at 8.18am local time on Wednesday, the agency said.
Shenzhou-24 will be China's 18th crewed launch and marks the first joint space flight mission conducted by Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of Beijing’s crewed space mission programme .
Mr Ali, 40, would spend about a week aboard the Chinese space station as a payload specialist and return to Earth aboard the Shenzhou 23 spacecraft, along with crew members Zhang Zhiyuan and Lai Ka-ying, returning after their six-month rotation.
“I’m not flying for myself; I carry the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hope of 250 million Pakistanis,” he told reporters at a press briefing on Tuesday.
The Pakistani astronaut hoped space cooperation between the two Asian countries would go from one astronaut in one flight to multiple joint missions to the Moon, Mars and beyond.
Mr Ali has trained for seven months since he was selected in April, including learning Mandarin for better communication with his crewmates.
“The labels and operating instructions aboard the spacecraft and space station are all in Chinese, and the Pakistani astronaut began training with virtually no foundation in the language," Mr Hongbo said.
On board the space station, Mr Ali would conduct scientific projects in the fields of biotechnology and materials, as well as an in-orbit experiment on photosynthetic microorganisms, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported.
“To every child who’s watching while I’m in orbit, look up at the sky and remember that I am up there with your dreams,” he said.
All facilities and equipment are in good condition for Wednesday’s launch, CMSA said.
The three-module Tiangong space station was completed in late 2022, and ever since, rotating six-month-long missions have kept the orbiting outpost constantly crewed ever since.
China hopes. to double the size of the space station in coming years, and facilitate more joint missions with crews from other countries.
This comes as the US and China are locked in a space race to the Moon, with both countries aiming to land boots on the lunar surface by 2030.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | U.S. Prepares to Raise Tariffs on China and Other Countries
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | U.S. Prepares to Raise Tariffs on China and Other Countries
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Benzinga and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue on some items through the links below.
President Donald Trump is preparing to raise tariffs on China and dozens of other countries just three weeks after Republicans lost their congressional majorities in an election dominated by concerns over the cost of living.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer could announce the results of a monthslong investigation into foreign industrial subsidies as soon as this week, with China likely facing some of the highest tariffs, the Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday.
Trump wants to restore much of his original tariff regime after the Supreme Court struck down his emergency-powers levies in February.
In March, Greer launched investigations into 16 economies over concerns that government subsidies give foreign manufacturers an unfair advantage over American companies.
Imports from the EU, Japan and South Korea, which currently face tariffs of between 10% and 12.5%, could see rates rise to as much as 15%, reflecting trade agreements negotiated with Trump last year.
China could face a steeper increase. Bloomberg reported in August that Washington was considering an additional 7.5% tariff, which would bring the rate to 20% from the current 12.5%. The final rate remains unclear.
An Associated Press survey found that roughly two-thirds of midterm voters believed Trump's tariffs had hurt the national economy.
"Tariffs have made everything too expensive," Texas Republican Sen. Ted Cruz wrote the day after the election.
Yet Greer told CNBC on Nov. 11 that Democratic gains had not changed America's trillion-dollar trade deficit or China's trillion-dollar trade surplus.
If Washington follows through on the 7.5% Bloomberg reported, China's general tariff rate would reach 20%, well above the 15% mark.
Yet traders on Polymarket give 77% odds that the rate stays between 5% and 15% at year-end, on nearly $17,000 in trading volume. The contract adds broad tariffs together but excludes product-specific duties.
Timing may explain why. The contract counts only tariffs in force by Dec. 31, not those merely announced.
When Washington imposed its forced-labor tariffs in July, seven weeks passed between proposal and implementation. If this week's announcement is a proposal, a similar timetable would push implementation into mid-January.
Diplomacy could also favor a delay. Trump met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen last week, and the countries' trade truce runs until Jan. 10.
The WSJ suggested that announcing tougher tariffs on China could help divert attention from the alleged chip-smuggling scandal at Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) , with lawmakers from both parties questioning what Washington knew about the smuggling and its broader approach to Beijing.
Despite that scrutiny, Trump personally pushed Nvidia's board to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang on Monday.

articles.title_orig: Trump appears to make millions from Nvidia intervention over Huang | First Thing
articles.title_zh: Trump appears to make millions from Nvidia intervention over Huang | First Thing
articles.content_orig:
Huang had resigned over an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.
President Donald Trump is taking credit for Jensen Huang's stunning return to Nvidia , saying in an interview on Monday that he spoke "directly and indirectly" to the company's board members about bringing Huang back as CEO.
The surprise move comes just days after Huang, who was accused of having an affair with a person alleged to be a Chinese intelligence asset, offered to rejoin the company and Nvidia said it did not intend to reinstate him .
"I spoke to them. Let me put it this way: And I convinced them. I made the deal," Trump, who had urged Huang's reinstatement publicly, said in a phone interview with CNBC .
The president called the decision by the Nvidia board to reinstate Huang as CEO and president "very exciting news."
"We have to protect our geniuses, and he's certainly a genius," Trump said.
Upon his reinstatement, Nvidia released a statement from Jensen Huang, saying, "I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution. I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment."
In a statement announcing Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia, Harvey C. Jones, chair of the company's board of directors, said, "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interest of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers.
Trump said a "very thorough investigation" by the U.S. government "exonerated" Huang and determined that he "did nothing wrong."
ABC News has reached out to the White House for clarification on which investigation Trump is referencing in the CNBC interview.
Trump did not say who on the Nvidia board he spoke to. He said the board asked for assurances that Huang was not a national security threat.
“They did ask for assurance on the national security threat, and we gave them assurance, at least with everything we know, and we know a lot. So, with everything we know, we gave them assurance,” Trump said.
Trump added, "But I can tell you the bigger threat would be losing the brain power of somebody like Jensen. That would be a threat to me. That would be a far bigger threat than anything we’re talking about."
The president said that he spoke to Huang after he was reinstated.
"I called him up and I said, 'I ask you to do one thing, Jensen, work hard,'" Trump said.
In an interview with The New York Times on Monday, Trump said he consulted with Attorney General Todd Blanche and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton before he "recommended" reinstating Jensen Huang to the Nvidia board.
“I had to go to them before I recommended this," Trump told the NYT. "Look, I can’t do this and then all of a sudden have somebody get indicted for, for whatever."
On Sunday, Clayton said on ABC's "This Week" that the investigation of Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese intelligence asset Jensen Huang (no relation) allegedly had an affair with and her former company, Megaspeed, remains under investigation. "And I'm going to await the outcome of that investigation," Clayton said.
Trump said Blanche and Clayton had been "studying it a long time," adding, "if there was something wrong, I wouldn’t have done it."
On Monday, the Commerce Department added Megaspeed to its Entity List, which prevents U.S. firms from doing business with listed companies without obtaining a special license.
Huang resigned from Nvidia on Nov. 12, amid investigations launched by the federal government and internally by Nvidia. His resignation came just five days after he sent a memo to colleagues acknowledging, "I was unfaithful to my wife."
In the memo, the 63-year-old Huang said, "I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it." He apologized to his colleagues, the Nvidia board, partners and shareholders, saying, "My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility."
Nvidia's board of directors announced that same day that it was launching an independent investigation into allegations that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort." The board said at the time that while it "has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information."
Shortly after Huang resigned, Trump called on the Nvidia board to recruit former Apple CEO Tim Cook to helm the company. But since then, he has made multiple public statements pushing for Huang's return to Nvidia.
A day after Huang memo was released by Nvidia, Trump said he spoke to Huang by phone. "He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy," Trump said, referring to Alice Huang.
Alice Huang is the former CEO of Megaspeed, a Singaporean company federal investigators are probing over alleged export control violations and the illicit transfer of advanced Nvidia AI chips to China.
In a Nov. 9 news conference, a Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson denied that Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset, calling the allegations "completely groundless and pure slander."
ABC News, citing sources familiar with U.S. intelligence gathered on the matter, reported on Monday that Alice Huang had been in touch with an official of China's top spy agency, a contact that occurred while she was in a relationship with Jensen Huang.
Before the Nvidia scandal became public, Trump was briefed twice on U.S. intelligence alleging that Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset, the first time in the fall of 2025, U.S. officials and sources briefed on the matter told ABC News.
On May 12 of this year, Secretary of State Marco Rubio shared intelligence with Trump on Air Force One showing Jensen Huang was in a relationship with Alice Huang, a U.S. official and two sources familiar with the matter have told ABC News.
Trump's briefing from Rubio, first reported in The New York Times, came shortly before Huang joined the president on a state visit to China, according to the U.S. official and sources. Huang was initially not listed among the CEOs joining Trump's China trip, but he joined the president's entourage in Alaska after news reports noted his absence. Trump later posted on his social media platform that Huang was on Air Force One with him.
Trump pursued getting Huang reinstated at Nvidia despite a rift that developed between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over why Megaspeed had not been blacklisted sooner as an alleged national security threat. Bessent blamed Lutnick for dragging his feet on the issue.
"Many other departments were pushing for this and Commerce had the pen," Bessent told Fox News.
Bessent told Fox News that questions remained unanswered about whether Nvidia's chips were illegally being diverted to China.
"I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent said.
In recent days, Trump had ramped up his public efforts to get Jensen Hung reinstated.
During a White House press conference on Friday, Trump said he and Chinese leader Xi Jinping discussed Jensen Huang during their talks in China last week. "I did discuss that with President Xi, and he said, ‘Oh, brilliant, brilliant! He’s a brilliant man.’ He is,” Trump told reporters. The president added, "I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance."
Following the decision by Nvidia's board to bring Huang back, Trump posted a statement on his Truth Social platform, praising the board for making "the correct and proper decision."
"The Country needs Jensen's leadership at Nvidia in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy," Trump wrote.

articles.title_orig: Russian governor detained in rare criminal case against regional leader
articles.title_zh: Russian governor detained in rare criminal case against regional leader
articles.content_orig:
Murmansk region Governor Andrei Chibis has been arrested on suspicion of fraud, embezzlement and illegal currency transactions, Russia’s Interior Ministry said Monday.
Chibis is the first sitting Russian governor to be arrested since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Interior Ministry spokeswoman Irina Volk said investigators suspect Chibis and several others of stealing more than 39 million rubles ($476,000) from the regional construction ministry’s budget and embezzling more than 1 billion rubles ($12.2 million) earmarked for rebuilding the highway between the Arctic towns of Apatity and Kirovsk.
Volk said investigators were also looking into suspected transfers to foreign bank accounts using falsified documents.
The state-run news agency TASS first reported Chibis’ arrest, citing law enforcement sources. A source told the Kommersant business daily that investigators were questioning him in Moscow.
Murmansk region Information Policy Minister Irina Brinkova said Chibis had traveled to Moscow on a scheduled work trip and was giving testimony in connection with the recent detentions of several regional officials.
The pro-Kremlin Telegram news channel Mash reported that he was arrested as he stepped off a plane in Moscow.
Investigators reportedly carried out unspecified “procedures” at the main building of the regional government on Monday, several days after law enforcement officers visited the regional construction ministry.
Sources told the local news outlet SeverPost that Chibis was questioned in connection with corruption cases in some of the region’s closed municipalities, where access is restricted. The Murmansk region is home to the main base of Russia’s Northern Fleet.
Authorities have opened several criminal investigations involving Murmansk regional officials and company executives in recent weeks.
Andranik Musatyan, the head of the Murmansk water utility, is under investigation, and Arseny Filippov, the deputy head of the Pechenga district, was detained.
Investigators are also looking into the suspected embezzlement of more than 271 million rubles ($3.3 million) during the construction of a kindergarten in the closed municipality of Alexandrovsk. Former municipal head Ilyas Mazitov is implicated in the case.
Chibis has governed the Murmansk region since 2019. He previously served as Russia’s deputy minister of construction, housing and utilities. He survived a stabbing attack in 2024, after which the assailant was sentenced to 13 years in prison.
The last arrest of a sitting Russian governor was in March 2021, when authorities detained Penza region Governor Ivan Belozertsev. He was later sentenced to 12 years in prison for taking bribes.

articles.title_orig: One every four minutes: 720,000 Russian soldiers killed since start of Ukraine war, new data suggests
articles.title_zh: One every four minutes: 720,000 Russian soldiers killed since start of Ukraine war, new data suggests
articles.content_orig:
Art: Arina Istomina / Mediazona
By the end of September 2026, at least 490,000 Russian soldiers had been killed in the war with Ukraine. These are people whose deaths have already been officially registered and appear in data leaked from a hack of Russia’s state statistics agency, Rosstat, shared with the journalists by Belarusian and Ukrainian hackers (Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow).
We are confident that this data is genuine. It holds up against our named list of the military dead (including entries not yet published), the national Probate Registry, other leaked civil registry databases, publicly available court rulings, and Rosstat’s own previously published statistics.
The Rosstat files also allowed us to double-check our earlier casualty estimates based on the Probate Registry—showing that those estimates were largely accurate, or even conservative when it comes to soldiers missing in action.
Accounting for delays in death registration, we estimate that the true number of Russian military dead stood at around 700,000 as of September.
This is a joint report with Meduza as part of our war mortality estimation project. The named list of the Russian military dead is compiled by Mediazona, the BBC’s Russian service, and a team of volunteers.
Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow announced their breach of Rosstat on November 1. They gained access not only to the agency’s website but also to its internal networks, exfiltrating terabytes of files—including mortality data that Rosstat stopped publishing in mid-2025. On November 8, the hackers shared the data with journalists.
Along with other media outlets, we received a database containing 29.7 million records, covering nearly all death registrations in Russia’s Unified State Register of Civil Status Records (EGR ZAGS) from the start of 2021 through August 2026. Rosstat receives these records in anonymised form: each entry includes demographic details, but no name.
On November 15, the hackers passed journalists a second batch of files: 15 million newer records from SMEV—Russia’s Interdepartmental Electronic Interaction System—covering death registrations through September 29, 2026. Outlets that published mortality figures based on the first leak only had access to data through August, which is why some published counts may differ.
The raw files contained multiple versions of the same death record, duplicates, and subsequent amendments, making data cleaning a nontrivial task. After processing both databases and removing errors and duplicates, we arrived at 11,658,178 unique death records. This total may still contain a small number of duplicates—for instance, where entries are incomplete or contain errors.
The raw mortality data comes from three sources. The first is a copy of a Rosstat MongoDB database called “deathFacts”, which stores anonymised death records. The hackers obtained this during their initial breach of Rosstat’s internal network, and its records run through early August 2026. The second is a separate dump from the same database accumulated while the hackers retained network access, though it only captures deaths through the end of August. The third source is a copy of a PostgreSQL database from the Interdepartmental Electronic Interaction System (SMEV), which continued receiving death records until the hackers lost access at the end of September 2026.
SMEV is the channel through which Rosstat receives already anonymised “raw” entries from the Unified State Register (EGR), which holds all vital records filed by Russian civil registry offices. Transfers to Rosstat via SMEV began in June 2023; prior to that, Rosstat appears to have received monthly spreadsheets separately from each region. Once SMEV was introduced, Rosstat’s internal database began populating automatically, with records undergoing additional processing—certain fields were stripped out while blank ones were filled in. For example, if the exact day of death was left blank in SMEV, Rosstat populated it with either the first of the month or the registration date of the death record itself.
Taken together, this gave us 29.7 million records in MongoDB from 2021 to late August 2026 (only around 100,000 entries date from earlier years) and 15 million “raw” records from June 2023 to late September 2026.
These entries do not correspond one-to-one with unique deaths: almost every death has multiple versions. In most cases, new versions reflect updated details or filled-in fields, such as a refined cause of death or previously missing dates. MongoDB contains roughly 11.7 million unique record numbers, while SMEV contains 6.7 million.
We retained only the latest active version of each record, which is typically the most complete. Occasionally, a record has no active version and its final entry is marked as revoked; we found about 286,000 such cases. This usually means the death was entered outside the official “reporting period” and excluded from published statistics. In 23,000 cases, we matched the revoked entry to a replacement record using dates of birth and death, birthplace, or death certificate number. In the remaining 263,000 cases, we kept the revoked version as evidence of a unique death.
The two databases overlap substantially: SMEV adds around 210,000 new death records and 60,000 updated versions of records already present in MongoDB.
In principle, every death registration carries a unique 21-digit vital record number following a strict format. The first digit denotes the EGR section (always 1 for vital records). The second denotes the record type—birth, marriage, divorce, death, etc. (7 for deaths). The next three digits encode the registration year; the following eight identify the civil registry office or issuing authority; and the next five give the sequential number for that record type at that office within the year (the first death recorded there in a given year is 00001). Digits 19 and 20 denote an “additional attribute,” and the final digit is a check digit.
“Additional attributes” describe the circumstances under which a record was created—such as digitising a paper record or entering a death while offline. As a result, the same death can end up sharing a sequential number while carrying a different 21-digit ID that differs only in the final three digits (the additional attribute and check digit). We merged records with identical 18-digit prefixes, matching dates of birth and death, and matching sex: 375,000 entries consolidated into 152,000 unique deaths (usually two or three versions of one death, and four in a single case).
In practice, however, civil registry offices sometimes issue two separate original records (coded 00 in the additional attribute) under the same sequential number. When entered into the online system, one may be assigned a different code, such as 10. In those cases, two completely different deaths share everything except the last three digits. In Rosstat’s database, we even found different individuals recorded under the exact same ID across different versions of a single record. In some instances we located new record numbers for these “overwritten” entries, but in roughly 1,000 cases we had to retain two distinct deaths under the same record number.
We also merged duplicates where the same death was re-registered at a different civil registry office—something that happened on a large scale with deaths initially registered in Rostov offices or declared by court ruling. On its own, the combination of date of birth and date of death identifies an individual fairly well: most pairs appear once or twice, very rarely five times, and more often only in isolated cases (typically when incomplete dates default to the first of the month or year). Any single additional matching field—birthplace, death certificate number (allowing for a one-character typo), place of death, or name where known—establishes an unambiguous match. articles.title_orig: Russia accuses NATO member Estonia of hostile actions ‘on the verge of unleashing open war’
articles.title_zh: Russia accuses NATO member Estonia of hostile actions ‘on the verge of unleashing open war’
articles.content_orig:
Russia's Foreign Ministry has lashed out at Estonia's government, accusing the NATO member of carrying out a range of "hostile actions" and putting the Baltic state "on the verge of unleashing open war" with Moscow.
The outburst underscores rising tensions between Russia and countries on NATO's eastern flank and comes after Estonia announced it will close its road border crossings with Russia from Dec. 1.
Russia's ministry said Monday it had lodged a formal protest to Estonia's chargé d'affaires, Marek Uhtegi, over Tallinn's decision to close its border crossings and accused the European Union member of imposing a naval blockade against Moscow.
"The Estonian diplomat was again informed that such provocative and extremely dangerous actions are on the verge of unleashing open war with Russia," the ministry said in a statement, describing measures taken by Estonian lawmakers as "Russophobic."
The ministry also accused Estonia of "tacitly" providing its airspace for Ukrainian drone flights and sharply criticized Tallinn's ban on the transit of Russian and Belarusian grain through Estonian territory, referring to a policy that was introduced at the start of October.
Estonia, which shares a 294-kilometer (183-mile) border with Russia, swiftly denied ever allowing its territory to be used for military operations by another country.
It also responded to Russia's allegations by saying the Kremlin appears to be seeking to divert attention from its own efforts to undermine European security.
"Russian missiles have reached Polish territory, Danish security services have identified an assassination plot in Denmark orchestrated by Russian intelligence services, merchant vessels in the Black Sea are under constant threat from Russian attacks, and in Estonia, an arson attack targeting a defence industry company, planned on the orders of Russian military intelligence, was foiled," Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said Monday.
"All this is happening while Russia continues its war of aggression against Ukraine," he added.
The rhetoric marks a significant escalation in tensions between Estonia and Russia. Tallinn, a staunch Ukraine ally, has frequently raised the alarm over sabotage attacks against NATO countries that have been supporting Kyiv since Russia launched the full-scale invasion of its neighbor in February 2022.
Earlier this month, Estonia said it would close road border crossings with Russia from Dec. 1 as it blames Moscow for an attempted "sabotage" of one of its defense companies, an allegation the Kremlin denies.
Tallinn has said the border closure will help to reduce Moscow's ability to conduct hostile activities against it and mitigate risks related to sanctions circumvention.
Ukraine has stepped up its attacks on Russian critical targets in recent weeks, damaging Russian President Vladimir Putin 's prized Crimea bridge , striking a Russian cargo ship in the Baltic Sea and destroying one of Russia's newest ships at a Libyan port .
The suspected Ukrainian attack on a Russian military-linked cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday prompted Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo to warn that the Ukraine war is "spilling over" into its immediate vicinity.
Finland, one of NATO's newest members , has also closed its land border crossings with Russia.
Ukraine's latest attacks on some of Russia's most protected targets have demonstrated Kyiv's capabilities to hurt Moscow even without ample U.S. military support, according to Mario Bikarski, senior Europe and Central Asia analyst for Verisk Maplecroft, a political risk consultancy.
"Ukraine will continue to look for ways to degrade not only Russia's economy, but also its geostrategic interests in the wider region, including the Mediterranean and the Middle East," Bikarski said.
The prospect of an imminent peace deal between Russia and Ukraine appears to be slim, Bikarski said, although "the latest surge in diplomatic activity and mounting losses for both sides signals an appetite from all sides to reach an agreement."

articles.title_orig: Denmark: Supreme Court backs hardline immigration law against 'non-Westerners'
articles.title_zh: Denmark: Supreme Court backs hardline immigration law against 'non-Westerners'
articles.content_orig:
Denmark’s Supreme Court has upheld a housing association’s decision to terminate 91 tenancy agreements in the Nøjsomhed complex in Helsingør, north of Copenhagen. This was intended to prevent the area from being designated a “hard ghetto” under Denmark’s 2018 law. The court also ruled that the eviction of immigrants and their descendants from so-called non-Western countries does not constitute discrimination in this case, Deutsche Welle reports .
The Supreme Court upheld a 2022 lower court ruling in the case of seven residents who challenged the termination of their leases. The court concluded that the law’s criterion is not based directly on ethnic origin: it divides people into two groups — immigrants and descendants of immigrants from non-Western countries, and all other persons. In the court’s view, both groups include people of different ethnic origins.
Danish law stipulates that social housing complexes with a high proportion of minority residents must be redeveloped, renovated and have their social composition changed. By 2030, at least 60% of apartments in such areas must be rented at market prices to residents whom the law classifies as Western.
More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram .
Danish Housing Minister Jacob Mark welcomed the ruling, stating that it strengthens security, social cohesion and integration. According to tenants’ associations, around 11,000 people across the country will have to be relocated to comply with the law’s requirements. The housing association involved in the case said it had taken measures to find new housing for the residents affected by the decision.
In Danish statistics, the category of non-Western countries includes all states except EU countries, as well as Andorra, Australia, the United Kingdom, Canada, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Monaco, New Zealand, Northern Ireland, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland, the United States and the Vatican.

articles.title_zh: 'A page out of the Chinese playbook,' How Trump's Nvidia intervention mirrors similar moves by China's government
articles.content_orig:
By JON MICHAEL RAASCH, WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT
Published: 10:10 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 06:09 EST, 24 November 2026
President Donald Trump has revealed what he told Jensen Huang right before the Nvidia chief executive was reinstated, following a 'spy' sex scandal that had forced him to resign.
'I talked to him [Jensen Huang] last night,' Trump told CNBC in an interview. 'I said, 'Jensen, just promise me one thing: You're going to work hard.
'You got brain, you got everything going. You're going to work hard, and if you work hard, there's nobody can beat you'.'
Nvidia's board of directors announced on Monday that the recently ousted boss would return to his position at the helm of the AI giant.
It prompted a stunning rally in Nvidia's shares – adding more than 30 per cent or nearly $1trillion (£763billion) to its value.
'The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO,' Trump wrote on social media.
The White House confirmed that Trump called in to the company's board of directors to advocate for Huang's return to leadership.
Huang's whirlwind firing and rehiring after multiple reported affairs, two with Nvidia subordinates and another with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang, have prompted a tumultuous few weeks for the AI firm and the US economy .
'The Country needs Jensen's leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy,' Trump said in a statement shortly after the company announced Huang's rehiring
Huang's whirlwind firing and rehiring after multiple reported affairs - two with Nvidia subordinates and another with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang - have prompted a tumultuous few weeks for the AI firm and US economy
Trump posted a meme on his Truth Social showing Huang holding up a red bra in a wild re-imagining of the iconic photo after Trump was shot by a would-be assassin in 2023
'He's apologized for indiscretion, which was unfortunate. That was probably that's what brought it to such a level, because sex sells fellas!' Trump said in a CNBC interview Monday morning.
'Now, [Jim] Cramer would not know that because he's a very, very, very committed person. But sex sells.'
Trump also claimed that Huang's wife, Lori, 64, has also decided to stand by her husband despite his infidelity.
'He's got a very, very, very good wife, and they've worked it out,' Trump told The New York Times. 'She's a fantastic woman.'
The president separately posted a meme on his Truth Social showing Huang holding up a red bra in a wild re-imagining of the iconic photo after Trump was shot by a would-be assassin in 2023.
Huang met his wife of 41 years at Oregon State University, when they were paired as lab partners in an electrical engineering class. He was 17 at the time.
The couple had already welcomed their two children, Madison and Spencer, by the time he co-founded Nvidia in 1993.
Both Madison and Spencer now hold key positions within high-priority business units at the company.
Lori is the president of the family's $9 billion charitable foundation and often accompanies her husband to events.
As the US's predominant AI company and microchip manufacturer, Nvidia has ballooned to become one of the most expensive US companies and a leader of cutting-edge computational development in the race against China for tech supremacy.
The recent string of damaging stories about Huang's personal conduct contributed to the company hemorrhaging over $1 trillion in market cap.
But the stock roared back to life, gaining over 25 percent on Monday following Trump's announcement that the company is not a national security risk.
'The Country needs Jensen's leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy,' Trump said in a statement shortly after the company announced Huang's rehiring.
'The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.

'The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.'
Huang is still the subject of an internal Nvidia investigation into his affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based data firm Megaspeed, which has been of particular concern within the administration.
There are suspicions that Alice Huang used her role at Megaspeed to convince the Nvidia boss to allow the sale of advanced chips to the Singapore-based firm before those same chips were used by Chinese AI firms, helping them effectively circumvent an export ban.
US officials noted that the Megaspeed executive speaks English well and has relationships with executives at the highest levels of the AI chip industry
'NVIDIA should continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company's compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security,' Trump said.
Nvidia said in its announcement on Monday that the probe into the 'foreign intelligence effort' will proceed and that the CEO 'fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.'
Additionally, the Nvidia boss is scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1 about the affair with the suspected spy.
The company has since established a national security and export control committee to identify possible compliance and security risks.
Trump has grown close with the Nvidia boss during his second term, repeatedly hosting Huang at the White House for ritzy state dinners and inviting him on state visits to China and the United Kingdom.
The president has also traded millions worth of Nvidia stock.
The Republican has made at least 108 transactions worth between $27.2 million and $97.9 million during his second term, according to a CNBC analysis of the president's Nvidia stock trades.
His official filing puts his Nvidia holdings at anywhere between $12.5million to $58million (£10million to £45million) at the end of 2025. The White House always says independent managers run Mr Trump's portfolio.
Huang returned Monday to Nvidia headquarters in Silicon Valley, and employees gathered in the building's atrium loudly cheered him on.
'I am going to be a better CEO the second time around,' Huang said.
The CEO, who will also serve as Nvidia president, said in a statement that he was 'honored' to return to the company and that he resumes the responsibility 'with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.'
He thanked board Chairman Harvey C Jones and interim CEO Colette Kress, who will return to her role as chief financial officer, as well as Nvidia's executive staff for their leadership during the brief period of disorder.
'I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support,' Huang´s statement said.
'Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can´t wait to get back to work.'
Fox News host Jesse Watters warned Trump that he will face massive Democratic backlash – and maybe even an impeachment attempt – after he saved the embattled Nvidia CEO.
'The Democrats are now licking their chops over the Jensen affair and Trump personally restoring [him] as CEO, even if it was to help the economy and the country,' the commentator said, noting: 'This gives [them] a lot of ammunition.'
'The Democrats will likely use the scandal to impeach,' he then warned.
'They will say the president is manipulating the market to enrich himself and his cabinet. And they are gonna say Jensen donated to the ballroom, so Trump saved his hide. They're gonna say Trump

articles.title_orig: Stock futures decline as Nvidia pulls back, giving back part of Monday’s rally: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock futures decline as Nvidia pulls back, giving back part of Monday’s rally: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia's remarkable stock comeback isn't done yet now that Jensen Huang has returned as CEO , CNBC's Jim Cramer said Monday.
"It's terrific to have this admittedly tarnished national treasure back leading Nvidia," the " Mad Money " host said. "It's kind of a miracle given the board's insistence that he would never get the CEO job again. But it's a miracle that saved the Nasdaq which, in turn, saved the market, at least for now."
Nvidia shares soared 31.5% on the news, fueling a broader rally in AI infrastructure stocks. The S&P 500 jumped 4.7%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite surged 6.5%, with both indexes posting their best days since April 2025. Monday's rebound erased nearly all of Nvidia's decline following Huang's Nov. 12 resignation amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one involving an alleged Chinese spy. Before the rally Monday, the stock had fallen in all trading sessions since his departure.
"Jensen's only one man, and Nvidia is only one company," he said. "But the truth is that Jensen is the linchpin that holds the AI solar system together, and Nvidia is the biggest beneficiary."
Cramer argued that Huang's reinstatement removes a major source of uncertainty for investors, strengthening the case for a higher valuation. The chipmaker delivered blockbuster quarterly results last week, raising its revenue growth outlook to 75%, but the results did little to stem the sell-off as investors remained concerned about its leadership.
"If it weren't for the Jensen overhang, and the insistence that Jensen could never come back, ... I think the stock would have been up significantly on that quarter," Cramer said.
Still, Cramer cautioned that Huang's return doesn't erase the broader headwinds facing Nvidia. Growing political opposition to data center construction following the midterm elections could slow AI infrastructure expansion, while uncertainty surrounding chip sales to China threatens a potential source of demand. Meanwhile, a more hawkish Federal Reserve has pressured technology stock valuations as investors brace for higher interest rates.
Those challenges, Cramer argued, make it difficult to justify a return to the $213 level Nvidia traded at before The New York Times first reported about Huang's relationship with a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence on Oct. 29. But with Huang back at the helm and the company's growth outlook intact, he said the stock deserves a higher valuation. The stock currently trades at roughly 10 times earnings estimates for Nvidia's fiscal 2028, according to FactSet.
"There is just no way that, with the return of Jensen, this stock deserves the same 10 times price to earnings multiple," Cramer said.
"These things are subjective, of course, but to start, let's say this stock deserves to trade at twelve times next year's earnings estimate, which would make this a $199 stock," Cramer said. "That's my target."

articles.title_orig: Beyond Competition: How China's Automotive Transformation Is Creating New Global Opportunities
articles.title_zh: Beyond Competition: How China's Automotive Transformation Is Creating New Global Opportunities
articles.content_orig:
China's automotive transformation is creating a new set of industrial capabilities that could benefit the global automotive industry as a whole.
Over the past decade, China has developed a highly interconnected automotive ecosystem, bringing together battery technology, intelligent driving, vehicle software, advanced manufacturing, and an increasingly sophisticated supply chain.
The significance of this transformation lies not only in the competitiveness of Chinese automakers, but also in the opportunities these capabilities create for companies around the world.
Volkswagen offers an interesting example. The group is targeting annual exports of around 300,000 vehicles from China by 2030. More importantly, it plans to introduce China-developed vehicle platforms and electronic architecture into selected overseas markets，which represents a meaningful evolution in the role of China within multinational automakers' global operations.
Image source: Volkswagen Group China
For decades, international automotive companies brought technology, manufacturing expertise, management practices, and engineering capabilities to China. These contributions played an important role in the development of China's automotive industry.
Today, we are beginning to see industrial capabilities flow in the other direction as well.
Chinese companies are expanding their manufacturing, engineering, and supply-chain operations overseas. Meanwhile, multinational companies are increasingly integrating China's innovation resources into their global development strategies.
This is not simply a reversal of traditional globalization. It is an evolution toward a more interconnected model of industrial collaboration.
Different markets still have their own strengths. China's rapidly evolving technology ecosystem can complement Europe's engineering expertise, Japan's manufacturing and quality management capabilities, and the growing industrial capacity of emerging markets.
The opportunity is not to replicate the Chinese automotive model everywhere, but to combine complementary capabilities and develop solutions that meet different local needs.
Of course, this transformation brings challenges. Companies must navigate regulatory differences, cultural expectations, financial pressures, and increasingly complex localization requirements.
These challenges also highlight the importance of deeper industrial collaboration, local capability building, and disciplined long-term investment.
For global automotive executives, the strategic question should therefore extend beyond how to compete with Chinese companies. It should also be about how to leverage China's industrial capabilities, integrate them with existing strengths, and create better products and sustainable businesses for consumers around the world .
In my view, the greatest value of China's automotive transformation will not be measured solely by the number of vehicles Chinese companies sell globally. It will also be measured by how much this transformation contributes to the evolution of the entire global automotive industry.
That is a much greater opportunity than winning a car war.

articles.title_orig: China works to suppress India's rise across multiple fronts - USCC
articles.title_zh: China works to suppress India's rise across multiple fronts - USCC
articles.content_orig:
China is "actively working to suppress India's rise," even as the relationship between the two major Asian powers has thawed in the past year, according to a U.S. panel that sees an opening for greater outreach to India.
On Nov. 18, a U.S. China Economic and Security Review Commission report said Beijing is applying military, economic, maritime, and other forms of pressure to constrain India .
China has recalled engineers and withheld equipment to slow India's electronics manufacturing, slashed pharmaceutical input prices to undercut new Indian plants, and imposed export controls on battery technology to impede the development of India's clean energy industry, the report said.
It added that these tensions offer the U.S. an opportunity to counter growing Chinese influence by building closer ties with India across key sectors such as pharmaceutical and defense.
Ties have improved since a deadly border skirmish in 2020, but experts told CNBC that trust is still thin between Beijing and New Delhi. However, they added that the uneasy peace with China is unlikely to make India align automatically with the U.S. as an ally.
The Indian foreign and commerce ministries and the Chinese foreign ministry did not respond to emails seeking comments.
The thawing in relations between India and China came amid industrial demand, as well as the need for "a whole lot of posturing for the U.S.," said Arpit Chaturvedi, South Asia advisor at strategic advisory firm Teneo.
Over the past year, India faced tariff pressures and needed to signal to Washington that its options remain open, including that of renegotiating relations with China, he explained, but added that as the trade deal with the U.S. is "close enough now," there is no pressing need for that signaling.
Further improvement in the relationship is also limited by reports of renewed border tensions between the two sides and Beijing's scant reciprocation on easing access to technology and people movement, he said.
Last month, an Indian military official said that confrontations with Chinese soldiers were ongoing across several locations along the country's northeastern border, even as top leaders from the countries met with fanfare at the BRICS Summit in September.
Another flash point was when Beijing put export controls on tunnel boring machines last month. "Our relations with China remain good, and if there aren't any new hurdles , they can improve further," India's Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal reportedly said after China's move to tighten TBM exports.
On Monday, a Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson reportedly said Beijing is ready to work with India to facilitate visa arrangements for business personnel from both sides amid reports that fewer Indian businessmen got visas to attend an annual trade fair in Shanghai.
The Chinese "actively disrupt" areas where India is trying to make progress in terms of moving global supply chains, developing advanced industrial technologies such as EVs, batteries, electronic components, and pharmaceutical ingredients, Pramit Pal Chaudhuri, South Asia practice head at Eurasia Group, told CNBC.
He added China is increasingly focused on containing India economically rather than through military overtures.
India's manufacturing push still relies on Chinese inputs, from electronics components and solar materials to rare earth magnets and specialized machinery. Between April and October, India imported goods worth $96.6 billion from China , up more than 30% from a year ago, as per commerce ministry data released earlier this month.
Its major imports from China include electronic goods, machinery, chemicals, transport equipment, iron and steel, and pharmaceutical products.
While India needs inputs for its manufacturing ambitions from Beijing and China values access to Indian markets, trust between the two sides is "still thin," according to Reema Bhattacharya, head of Asia research at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, citing a large trade imbalance and overlapping interests in South Asia and the Indian Ocean as additional issues.

articles.title_orig: Afghan women with UK university offers 'heartbroken' after visas stopped
articles.title_zh: Afghan women with UK university offers 'heartbroken' after visas stopped
articles.content_orig:
Saurav Das said that he was supposed to deliver a series of lectures in the UK
A leader of India's "cockroach" party has said that immigration officials at Delhi airport stopped him from flying to the UK, where he was set to attend a series of events.
Saurav Das said he was supposed to board a flight on Tuesday at 01:00 local time (19:30 GMT on Monday) but was told by immigration officers that his passport had been "flagged".
It is not clear yet why Das's passport was flagged. The BBC has reached out to the federal home ministry, Delhi police and airport officials for comment.
Das, who rose to prominence in India earlier this year after Gen Z-led protests , said that he had been invited by the Oxford Union to speak about the movement.
He said that he was also scheduled to speak at other universities in Cambridge and Edinburgh.
"Indian students put their heart and soul to organise the events but this anti-intellectual [government] was scared of me going to these prestigious institutions," he wrote on X.
A federal home ministry spokesperson directed the BBC to airport authorities and the Delhi police for comment on Das's allegations.
Ratna Singh, another leader of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), said in a post on X that she and Das had been invited by the Oxford Union but that her visa had been rejected a few days ago.
"The manner in which Saurav was not allowed to board today raises deeply troubling questions about the state of freedom of expression and the space being allowed for young voices in this country," she wrote.
Das, a former journalist, became one of the faces of the CJP - a Gen Z-led movement that began as satire but has since emerged as a youth-led pressure group.
In July, protests spearheaded by the CJP over exam paper leaks led to the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan .
In October, CJP leaders including Das were among thousands of people detained by the police for trying to hold protests demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Kumar and the Election Commission have denied wrongdoing.
The same month, Das and Ashutosh Ranka, another CJP leader, were jailed for seven days after being arrested for trespassing at a banned protest site in Delhi.
Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of CJP, wrote on X that if Das "had looted a bank or committed financial fraud", he may have been allowed to fly to London, referring to billionaire bank-loan defaulters who have left India.
There have been other instances in recent years of people being prevented from boarding flights.
In September 2025, Bhanu Tatak, an environmental and anti-dam activist from India's north-eastern Arunachal Pradesh state, was stopped from boarding a flight to Dublin.
In March 2022, Rana Ayyub, an investigative journalist and outspoken critic of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government, was also stopped from boarding a flight to London at the Mumbai airport. She was due to speak at different events on media freedom and the targeting of journalists.

articles.title_orig: Trump Administration Imposes Sanctions on Megaspeed, Singaporean Firm at Center of Nvidia Scandal
articles.title_zh: Trump Administration Imposes Sanctions on Megaspeed, Singaporean Firm at Center of Nvidia Scandal
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration on Monday added the company at the heart of the Nvidia scandal, Megaspeed, to a trade blacklist designed to prevent it from obtaining US-made semiconductors.
The Singapore-based company was added to the Commerce Departmentâs entity list on Monday afternoon, plans that were first reported by Semafor.
The addition means that no US company can sell certain technologies, including semiconductors, to Megaspeed or its foreign affiliates without obtaining a license from the US government. The news comes the same day the Nvidia board voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as its CEO, after President Donald Trump implored them to do so. Huang resigned less than two weeks ago amid scrutiny over his extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
According to a filing from Commerceâs Bureau of Industry and Security posted to the Federal Register Monday afternoon, seven total entities were added to the list from Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand, including various affiliates of Megaspeed, MSFusion, Speedmatrix, Apex Enterprise Solutions, and Swiftdata. âThese additions are being made because of the significant risk of these entities being or becoming involved in the diversion of advanced computing commodities to unauthorized end uses or end users,â the filing reads. âThese entities will be added with a license requirement for all items subject to the [Export Administration Regulations] and licenses will be reviewed under a presumption of denial.â
Technology exports already en route to the targeted companies will be allowed to go through, the filing suggests.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been under pressure to place Megaspeed on the departmentâs entity list from others inside the administration, tensions that became public after news broke of Huangâs relationship with Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy who was an executive at Megaspeed. The Justice Department is investigating whether Megaspeed violated US export controls by shipping Nvidia chips to China.
Earlier this month, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said his agency along with the Pentagon, the State Department, and the US Trade Representative had backed putting Megaspeed on the entity list âfor monthsâ but that âCommerce holds the pen.â Bipartisan lawmakers have pressed Lutnick to put Megaspeed on the entity list and explain his decisions around Nvidia, Megaspeed, and chip export controls.
âThe Commerce Department placed Megaspeed on the Entity List. This makes it unlawful to export any US-origin goods, software, or technology to Megaspeed,â BIS spokesman Thomas Wackman told Semafor. âIt is also now unlawful to export advanced SI chips to Megaspeed, even if the chips are produced outside the United States. Commerce will continue to vigorously enforce export controls, including these new Entity Listings.â

Its major imports from China include electronic goods, machinery, chemicals, transport equipment, iron and steel, and pharmaceutical products.
While India needs inputs for its manufacturing ambitions from Beijing and China values access to Indian markets, trust between the two sides is "still thin," according to Reema Bhattacharya, head of Asia research at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, citing a large trade imbalance and overlapping interests in South Asia and the Indian Ocean as additional issues.

articles.title_orig: Mayanot Jerusalem Honors Its Partners at Rooftop Celebration
articles.title_zh: Mayanot Jerusalem Honors Its Partners at Rooftop Celebration
articles.content_orig:
The Mayanot Institute of Jewish Studies in Jerusalem hosted a rooftop celebration honoring its supporters and bringing together alumni and friends from around the world. Full Story, Video
The Mayanot Institute of Jewish Studies in Jerusalem hosted a rooftop celebration honoring its supporters and bringing together alumni and friends from around the world. Full Story, Video
The Mayanot rooftop has become a Jerusalem landmark, with its breathtaking view of the city, and stunning sunsets. Sitting at the entrance to the city, a stone’s throw from the Machane Yehuda market, and right across from Kraft Stadium, the Mayanot Institute of Jewish Studies always has its lights on and is filled with students and teachers learning at all hours of the day.
Recently, we gathered on the rooftop to honor those who helped build and create the Institute, with live music by the Solomon Brothers, and an evening dedicated to our partners and friends. We welcomed David and Eda Schottenstein , who dedicated Mayanot’s beautiful lobby; Abe and Nily Edynast , who donated the main tzedakah box; and Yitzchak Yoel and Roberta Schoen , who dedicated the library in the Beit Midrash.
Rabbi Kasriel Shemtov , Director of Mayanot, introduced Mr. Yitzchak Yoel Schoen for the dedication of the Beit Midrash library, and emphasized, “Torah is something we take with us even when we leave the walls of this yeshiva, and Mayanot endeavors to give students the tools to learn on their own so Torah learning becomes part of their life journey.”
Reb Yitzchak Yoel shared, “The real joy comes not from a plaque like this, but seeing the people use the books daily, and that’s what [Mayanot] is all about.”
David Schottenstein added that those who give to Mayanot are giving “to a place that wants to give to others. You’re building homes, you’re building Jewish homes.”
Friends and family from all 30 years of Mayanot came from around the globe to celebrate. Ken Schuckman , who studied at Mayanot in 1997, came with his sons and said, “Mayanot is probably one of the most popular places in the world! They are still my rabbis and my brothers. And now, look at this. It’s absolutely magnificent. I feel so blessed and proud to be here tonight.”
Israeli Channel 14 journalist, Yedidya Meir , said, “What’s beautiful is not the roof; it’s what happens under the roof.”  That is exactly what Mayanot is: a home for learning and growth, and for following the Rebbe’s mission of spreading light.
Eli S., a lone soldier serving in a combat unit who lives in the Mayanot dorms, said, “I came, and it was the greatest decision I’ve ever made. When I am on base, I can’t wait to get out and come home to Mayanot because it’s such an incredible environment here. This is the greatest way one who wants can contribute to lone soldiers.”
Rabbi Shlomo Gestetner , Dean of Mayanot, spoke about how every single Jew can become someone who learns Torah on a regular basis, and we have the honor and privilege of starting many journeys here at Mayanot.
We are looking forward to many more celebrations here in Jerusalem, at Mayanot, both on the rooftop and within our halls.

NATO will deploy an AWACS early-warning system aircraft to Poland as part of its response to ⁠three missiles landing in the country on the military alliance’s eastern flank, a Polish deputy defense minister said on Monday.
Three Russian Kh-101 missiles ⁠landed in Poland ​on ⁠Friday, prosecutors said, adding to fears that Russia’s war in Ukraine could spill ⁠into NATO territory.
“An AWACS early-warning aircraft ​will ⁠be made available to Poland,” ‌ Pawel Zalewski told reporters after a NATO meeting in Brussels. “This is a very ‌good system that gives us ‌even deeper... operational awareness which allows us to respond better to this kind of threat.”
With their distinctive ⁠nine-meter-wide radar domes, NATO’s 14 Airborne Warning and Control System aircraft have served as the alliance’s eyes in the sky since 1982.
Based at Geilenkirchen air base in Germany, the fleet has played an important role ‌in surveillance missions along NATO’s eastern ​flank since Russia launched its ‌full-scale invasion of Ukraine in ⁠2022.
In a conflict, they can ⁠provide a common radar picture for allied fighters, ships ‌and control ​centers, while directing NATO combat ‌jets to their ​targets.

articles.title_orig: Nintendo Switch Online finally adds new option fans have been asking for after nearly a decade
articles.title_zh: Nintendo Switch Online finally adds new option fans have been asking for after nearly a decade
articles.content_orig:
As part of the latest update on the Nintendo GameCube – Nintendo Classics app, a much-requested feature has finally been added for those playing via Switch Online.
Since the launch of the service in 2018, many fans have been annoyed by the borders present whenever they play a classic title. Unfortunately, there was no way to turn them off.
This didn’t just affect the GameCube app. The same issue has been present with the NES, SNES, and N64 counterparts, for example.
Thankfully, starting today, you can at least turn off the borders in GameCube games. To do so, head to “Extra Elements Display” in the settings, where you’ll find the “Border graphics” option. This can be switched on or off at any point.
Here’s a comparison between the two options:
This may not seem like a big deal for some people, but for others, it’s very significant. Some feel that they’re distracting and take away from the experience.
There are a couple of things to point out here. First, even with the border turned off, your Nintendo Switch Online icon will still be present. Additionally, so far the option is only available in Nintendo GameCube – Nintendo Classics – though it’s very likely we’ll see it roll out to the other apps at some point.
In case you missed it, Nintendo GameCube – Nintendo Classics just added Wave Race: Blue Storm today. You can find out what else is happening with Nintendo Switch Online .
Will you be trying the new border option for yourself or do you simply not care? Let us know in the comments.
